title: Modeling and analysis of hybrid systems
text:
Modeling and analysis of hybrid systems — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Hybrid systems are systems with mixed discrete and continuous behaviour. Typical examples
are physical systems which continuously evolve over time and which are controlled by some
discrete controller, e.g., a chip or a computer.
The behaviour of hybrid systems is often safety-critical. For example, in case of an accident
an airbag can save the life of the car driver, but only if the airbag reacts in time. To assure
the correct functioning of such safety-critical hybrid systems, their automatic synthesis and
analysis is of high importance.
In the lecture we first introduce hybrid automata to model hybrid systems and logics to specify
safety and lifeness properties of the models. We introduce different classes of hybrid automata
with increasing expressive power. For each class we discuss whether the reachability problem
is decidable, and develop algorithms for their analysis. Finally we discuss methods for
abstraction and for the over-appoximative representation of state sets and show how they can
be used for reachability analysis.
Contents:
• Discrete, continuous and hybrid systems, examples
• Modeling formalism: hybrid automata
• Some important features: time determinism, time divergence, Zeno-behaviour, stability
etc.
• Interesting classes of hybrid automata: timed automata, rectangular automata, linear
hybrid automata, non-linear hybrid automata
• Analysis: model checking, abstraction, approximation
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know

title: The Graph Isomorphism Problem
text:
The Graph Isomorphism Problem — content and learning objectives: Content: The graph isomorphism problem is one of the most important
open problems in theoretical computer science. Over the last 50 years,
numerous partial results habe been obtained, building on techniques
from different branches of theoretical computer science and
mathematics. The course covers highlights of the research on the graph
isomorphism problem, starting from early results from the 1970s to
recent results. Each of the results will be embedded into an
introduction to its techniques and context.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• knowledge in the research area of the graph isomorphism problem and the techniques
used
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• learn advanced techniques from various fields of theoretical computer science
(algorithms, complexity theory)
• learn advanced techniques from adjacent areas of mathematics (graph theory,
algorithmic group theory)
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• combine and apply these techniques in the context of a current research topic

title: Parameterized Algorithms
text:
Parameterized Algorithms — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Many practical problems turned out to be NP-hard and in the classical view they are therefore
"intractable". ;Parameterized algorithms aim at exploiting that practical instances are not
as hard as worst case instances. In this lecture, you will learn about such parameterized
algorithms and general techniques for their design. We emphasize those techniques that lead
to algorithms that are useful in practice. There are also some techniques that easily show
that some problems can indeed be solved by a parameterized algorithm, but the running
times will be very high. Finally, there are techniques that show that certain problems probably
cannot have parameterized algorithms at all based on a complexity theory for parameterized
problems.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• fundamentals of parameterized complexity theory
• parameterized algorithms and design methods for important problems
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• apply methods such as bounded search trees, iterative compression, treewidth-based
methods, color coding, kernels, and other standard techniques to an appropriate
problem
• prove that a problem is unlikely to be solved by a parameterized algorithm
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• identify the most suitable method for a parameterized problem and solve it accordingly

title: Mathematical Logic II
text:
Mathematical Logic II — content and learning objectives: set theory and foundations of mathematics, ordinal and cardinal numbers, axiom of choice,
Gödel's incompleteness theorems, introduction to model theory, fixed-point logics
Students shall gain insight into the foundational problems of mathematics (and computer
science) and understand the benefits and limitations of the axiomatic system ZFC as the set-
theoretic foundation of mathematics. The methods and tools from the course "Mathematical
Logic" shall be built upon and extended. In particular, students shall be introduced to working
with ordinal numbers, transfinite induction and basic model-theoretic methods. In addition to
the formal systems covered in "Mathematical Logic", the focus lies in particular on fixed-point
logics (the modal μ-calculus and LFP). The goal is to understand the expressive power of
those formalisms and to learn how to express mathematical concepts in fixed-points logics.

Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• develop and apply decision procedures effectively
• determine when and how these methods can be applied to solve problems in various
areas of computer science
• communicate scientific problems precisely
• recognize the value of formal methods and apply them with increased motivation

title: Satisfiability Checking
text: Satisfiability Checking — prerequisites: Knowledge from the modules "Mathematical logic", as well as "Algorithms and data structures".

title: Logics for Reasoning about Uncertainty
text:
Logics for Reasoning about Uncertainty — content and learning objectives: Description of various logical systems for reasoning about issues that arise when the available
data and/or observed events are uncertain, unknown, or unreliable. This includes aspects
of quite different nature such as knowledge, dependence and independence, imperfect
information, randomness. Connections to decision theory, probabilistic databases, provenance,
and games.
Understanding of the differences between various forms of uncertainty and the logical
methods for dealing with them. Mastering the methods for analyzing the expressive power and
algorithmic properties of the appropriate logical systems.

text:
Logics for Reasoning about Uncertainty — prerequisites: Kenntnisse aus der Vorlesung Mathematische Logik

title: Stochastic Games
text:
Stochastic Games — content and learning objectives: The course offers an introduction to stochastic games. In such a game, in each round the
players independently choose their actions, and the next state is then determined by a
probability distribution that depends on the chosen actions.
Some basic results and algorithms for stochastic games with different types of winning
conditions will be presented.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• the model of stochastic games and its basic properties
• algorithmic methods for solving stochastic games
• mathematical methods for dealing with stochastic games
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• use stochastic games as a model
• apply essential mathematical and algorithmic methods for dealing with stochastic
games
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• use stochastic games as a model
• apply mathematical and algorithmic methods for dealing with stochastic games

title: Stochastic Games

title: Advanced Algorithmics
text:
Advanced Algorithmics — content and learning objectives: The course presents an introduction into several central areas of advanced algorithmics, as
for instance: Approximation algorithms; Online algorithms; Meta-heuristics; Exact algorithms;
Parametrized algorithms; Tractable special cases; Randomized algorithms; Parallel and
distributed algorithms; I/O-efficient algorithms. Each area is treated in an independent chapter
that explains the main ideas, shows the fundamental definitions and central results, and
summarizes the goals and the methodology.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• basic notions and concepts in advanced algorithmics
• the most important algorithms in this area and can explain them
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• critically discuss algorithmic problems
• apply the central methodology of the area
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• model algorithmic problems
• apply methods from advanced algorithmics to solve such problems

title: Advanced Algorithmics
text:
Advanced Algorithmics — prerequisites: Knowledge of Data Structures and Algorithms; Efficient algorithms; Computability and
Complexity

title: Provenance Analysis and Semiring Semantics for Logics and Games
text:
Provenance Analysis and Semiring Semantics for Logics and Games — content and learning objectives: Algebraic and order-theoretic foundations of commutative semirings. Semiring semantics for
database query languages (relational algebra, datalog,...) and logics (first-order logic, modal
logics, fixed-point logics, ...), with applications to confidence scores, cost computation, and
access control. General provenance analysis by semirings of polynomials and formal power
series. Model-theoretic and algorithmic properties of semiring semantics. Strategy analysis in
finite and infinite games.
Knowledge: Commutative semirings and their algebraic properties. Semiring interpretations.
Semiring valuations of logical statements, database queries, and positions in games.
Fundamental facts about the model theory and complexity of semiring valuations.
Skills: The student will be able to evaluate logical statements in various semirings, to track
which combinations of basic facts are responsible for the truth of a complex statement, to apply
semiring valuations in the analyis of issues such as confidence, cost, access control, proof
counts, or repairs, and to analyse the available strategies in games via semiring valuations.
;;
Competences: The student will be able to make use of semiring semantics for a detailed
analysis of broad classes ;; of logical systems, database queries, and finite or infinite games.

title: Provenance Analysis and Semiring Semantics for Logics and Games

title: Fixpoints and Induction in Logic and Computer Science
text:
Fixpoints and Induction in Logic and Computer Science — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): This course is about the proof method of induction, and about the theory of fixpoints on
ordered structures, complete lattices in particular. Topics covered are:
• Induction on natural numbers, structural induction, well-founded induction
• Tarski's fixpoint theorem for monotonic functions on complete lattices and variations on
complete partial orders
• Examples from games, probability theory (Markov chains and decision processes),
program semantics and verification, automata theory and formal languages
• Computation of fixpoints by iteration on finite lattices
• Characterization of fixpoints on infinite lattices for continuous functions and arbitrary
functions
• Ordinal numbers, transfinite induction, well-ordering theorem
• First-order logic with fixpoints
• The role of induction in incompleteness theorem for Peano arithmetic
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• the relation between inductive proofs and least fixpoints
• the central role of fixpoints in various areas of computer science
• how to identify order structures in different areas of computer science and discrete
mathematics, particularly complete lattices
• how to use the corresponding fixpoint theorems
• strategies for computing fixpoints on finite lattices
• the role of induction in incompleteness results for first-order logic
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to

title: Fixpoints and Induction in Logic and Computer Science
text:
Fixpoints and Induction in Logic and Computer Science — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): • the role of induction in incompleteness results for first-order logic
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• apply fixpoint theorems in different contexts of computer science and discrete
mathematics
• compute fixpoints on finite lattices using appropriate strategies
• use induction to derive results in first-order logic, including incompleteness results
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• effectively use inductive proofs and fixpoint theorems in computer science and discrete
mathematics
• apply these concepts to solve problems in areas such as program verification,
optimization, and logic
• recognize and address the challenges related to fixpoints and induction in both
theoretical and practical applications in computer science

title: Dynamical Processes on Networks
text:
Dynamical Processes on Networks — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Many real-world systems may be described as a network of dynamically interacting entities.
We interact with each other in a social contact network, over which rumours as well as
pathogens cam spread; electrical energy is delivered by the power grid; the Internet enables
almost instantaneous world-wide interactions; our economies rest upon a complex network of
inter-dependencies spanning the globe. Networks are ubiquitous in complex biological, social,
engineering, and physical systems. Understanding the dynamics of these systems is essential
if we are to redesign them, or guide/control them towards different behaviours. Networked
control problems abound and include multi-user communication, distributed computation and
sensing, swarming, flocking, and synchronization.
This course provides a (mathematical) introduction to such network dynamical systems.
We discuss a selection of fundamental dynamical phenomena over interconnected network
systems, e.g., consensus and disagreement in averaging systems, epidemic spreading
dynamics, opinion formation models and synchronization of coupled oscillators and networked
control systems.
Knowledge: After successful completion of this module, students know
• distributed dynamical systems on networks, including both linear and nonlinear
processes
• linear processes such as consensus dynamics, distributed averaging, network diffusion
models, and opinion formation models

title: Dynamical Processes on Networks
text:
Dynamical Processes on Networks — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): processes
• linear processes such as consensus dynamics, distributed averaging, network diffusion
models, and opinion formation models
• nonlinear processes such as epidemic spreading (SI, SIS, SIR) and synchronization
processes
Skills: After successful completion of this module, students will be able to
• model a variety of systems as networks
• analyze key features of the dynamics of such dynamical network systems using
algebraic graph theory
• relate structural properties of the network to observed dynamical behaviors
• simulate and analyze the dynamics of such systems using Python code
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in this module, students will be
able to
• use networks as a language to communicate across different application domains
• analyze and implement simple models for network dynamics across various domains

title: Post-quantum cryptography
text:
Post-quantum cryptography — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): • Foundations
• Mathematical foundations of post-quantum security
• Quantum computing (programming quantum computers)
• Cryptographic security proofs
• Quantum random-oracle model
• Insecurity of existing cryptography
• RSA / discrete logarithm based cryptosystems

versions

title: Introduction to Quantum Computing
text:
Introduction to Quantum Computing — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): What are quantum computers? Are they magic computers that can compute everything faster?
Or are they some science-fiction that has nothing to do with reality? How do they work?
What can they do? In this lecture, we will introduce the basics of quantum computing from
the computer science perspective. We will understand how quantum mechanics allows us
to compute some problems faster (and some not), how to program a quantum computer,
and what the challenges are. There will be a mix of mathematical foundations, and applied
quantum computer programming.
Content:
• Mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics
• How do quantum computers work?
• How are quantum computers built? (Physical implementations.)
• Why are quantum computers difficult (problems with noise)
• Programming a quantum computer (Writing your own quantum programs.)
• Quantum algorithms:
• Simple basic algorithms
• Grover’s algorithm (“database” search)
• Shor’s algorithm (factoring, etc.)
• Possibly more
• Quantum simulation (simulating physical processes with a quantum computer)
• The course comes with both theory and with programming exercises, to run on
simulated (or real) quantum computers.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module students know
• the basic mathematics of quantum computing
• how quantum computers work
• how quantum computers are built
• how the most important quantum algorithms work
• what the problems are with building quantum computers
• how quantum computers are programmed

title: Introduction to Quantum Computing
text:
Introduction to Quantum Computing — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): • how the most important quantum algorithms work
• what the problems are with building quantum computers
• how quantum computers are programmed
• how quantum computers relate to the simulation of physical systems
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• compute what a quantum program does (on paper)
• program quantum computers (simple programs)
• understand research papers introducing quantum algorithms
• understand why quantum computers cannot just do everything faster
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• understand claims about quantum computers (recognize obvious nonsense)
• put modern developments in quantum computing into context
• follow advanced quantum computing related courses
• join projects working on the software-side of quantum computing

title: Near-term Quantum Computation
text:
Near-term Quantum Computation — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): This lecture is an interdisciplinary (computer science, physics, mathematics) introduction to
modern algorithmic challenges as they occur in the usage of near-term quantum computing
hardware. After reviewing the basics of quantum computation and algorithms we will cover the
limitation of current quantum computing hardware from a computer scientist’s point of view.
Next, we will discuss algorithms for near-term quantum computers, before we turn to quantum
compilation, i.e. algorithms for the optimal mapping of quantum algorithms to real quantum
computers. Finally, we will cover the basics of quantum error correction and mitigation.
This lecture is an interdisciplinary (physics, computer science, mathematics) introduction
quantum algorithms for near-term quantum computing hardware. After reviewing the basics of
quantum computation and algorithms we will cover the limitation of current quantum computing
hardware. Next, we will discuss algorithms for near-term quantum computers, which is the
main focus of the lecture. Finally, we turn to quantum compilation, i.e. algorithms for the
optimal mapping of quantum algorithms to real quantum computers, as well as quantum error
mitigation and correction.
Knowledge: ;After successful completion of the module students know
• basics and limitations variational quantum algorithms on near-term (noisy) quantum
computers as well as quantum annealers
• how to map applications to near-term (noisy) quantum computers

title: Near-term Quantum Computation
text:
Near-term Quantum Computation — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): computers as well as quantum annealers
• how to map applications to near-term (noisy) quantum computers
• basic concepts of quantum compilation

• perform research on application focused quantum algorithms for near-term quantum

title: Combinatorial Optimisation in Scientific Practise

top of proving or disproving statements, the abilities to work with literature, describe a

participation.

• differences between various types of publications

appropriate
• perform basic computational studies on the RWTH HPC cluster and present the results
in oral and written form

able to
• work scientifically in the area of combinatorial optimization under expert guidance

title: Algorithmic Foundations of Datascience
text:
Algorithmic Foundations of Datascience — content and learning objectives: The course is an introduction to a wide range of algorithmic
techniques that are used in data science, with a focus on mathematical
and theoretical aspects such as a careful complexity
analysis. Starting with mathemtical foundations from probability
theory, information theory, and linear algebra, the course covers
typical algorithmic techniques for data analysis tasks as well as
typical algorithmic techniques applied in big-data scenarios, such as
streaming algorithms and algorithms for compute clusters.
Knowledge: ;After successful completion of the module, students know:
• a broad range of data science algorithms and their mathematical foundations
Skills: ;After successful completion of the module, students will be able to:
• develop a theoretical understanding of algorithmic efficiency and complexity in data
science scenarios
• apply techniques to analyze algorithms within this domain
Competencies: ;Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to:

Computer science foundations from data structures and algorithms,

title: Mathematical heuristics for discrete optimization problems
text:

title: Theory of Distributed Systems
text:
Theory of Distributed Systems — content and learning objectives: • Algorithms in message-passing systems
• Leader election and consensus

• Contagion and Distributed Network Dynamics

title: Theory of Distributed Systems

title: Optimization and Uncertainty
text:
Optimization and Uncertainty — content and learning objectives: Optimization problems with uncertainty about the input arise in many areas of modern
computing systems. Often probabilistisc assumptions about (parts of) the input is available. In
this course, we discuss algorithmic techniques that can be used for such scenarios and come
with provable performance guarantees. Topics include, e.g., stochastic online optimization,
elementary stopping problems and combinatorial extensions, Markov decision processes,
probing problems, online convex optimization and multi-armed bandit problems, or game-
theoretic scenarios.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• theoretical understanding of stochastic uncertainty models and optimization algorithms
along with their limitations
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• clear conception of the assumptions underlying models of uncertainty and their
algorithms
• ability to give estimates on the approximation quality of the derived solutions
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• application of theoretical insights to support the selection of suitable algorithms in
generalized scenarios and for new optimization tasks

title: Optimization and Uncertainty
text: Optimization and Uncertainty — prerequisites: Good knowledge of data structures and algorithms, stochastics and linear programming.

title: Cryptography
text:
Cryptography — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): The module covers the following topics:
• Foundations: security goals, attack models, and the game-based security framework
• Pseudorandomness: one-way functions, pseudorandom generators, and
pseudorandom functions
• Symmetric cryptography: secret-key encryption, CPA and CCA security, message
authentication codes, authenticated encryption
• Hash functions: collision resistance, the random oracle model
• Public-key cryptography: key encapsulation, public-key encryption (IND-CPA, IND-
CCA), digital signatures
• Hardness assumptions: discrete logarithm, RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and related problems;
introduction to lattice-based assumptions
• Security proofs: reduction-based arguments, hybrid proofs, and standard proof
techniques
In addition, the module covers selected advanced topics, which may vary by semester.
Possible topics include zero-knowledge proofs, post-quantum cryptography, identity-based
encryption, secure computation, or cryptographic applications in decentralized systems.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• the fundamental goals of cryptography, including confidentiality, integrity, and
authenticity
• formal security definitions for core cryptographic primitives such as symmetric
encryption, hash functions, MACs, and public-key encryption
• the mathematical foundations underlying cryptographic constructions, including
number theory, algebra, and computational complexity

title: Cryptography
text:
Cryptography — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): • the mathematical foundations underlying cryptographic constructions, including
number theory, algebra, and computational complexity
• standard cryptographic building blocks (e.g. pseudorandom functions, one-way
functions, digital signatures) and their provable security guarantees
• the most important hardness assumptions (e.g. discrete logarithm, RSA problem,
LWE) that modern cryptography relies on
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• precisely formulate security definitions using the game-based or simulation-based
paradigm
• follow and verify formal security proofs, including reduction-based arguments
• analyze the security properties of cryptographic schemes with respect to a given
adversary model
• develop simple game-based security proofs
• assess the validity and tightness of security reductions
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• independently study and evaluate cryptographic constructions and their security proofs
from the research literature
• reason rigorously about the security of unfamiliar cryptographic schemes
• identify the assumptions a scheme's security relies on and critically assess their
plausibility

title: Cryptography

title: Advanced Topics in Logic
text:
Advanced Topics in Logic — content and learning objectives: The lecture covers selected topics in logic that are particularly important for computer science.
Both classical topics and current developments are taken into account. Examples of topics are
the following:

• Decidable and undecidable theories
• Intuitionistic logic

include both model-theoretic (semantic) and proof-theoretic (syntactic) methods.

able to
• better assess the applicability and the limitations of formal logical methods.

title: Advanced Topics in Logic

title: Foundations of Learning on Graphs
text:
Foundations of Learning on Graphs — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Graph-structured data is ubiquitous across application domains ranging from chemo- and
bioinformatics to image and social network analysis. To develop successful machine learning
algorithms, we need techniques that map the rich information inherent in the graph structure
to a vectorial representation in a meaningful way—often called graph embeddings. Roughly,
the first two-thirds of this class offers an overview of recent results shedding light on graph
embeddings' theoretical properties, i.e., their expressivity and generalization performance,
focusing on graph neural networks. In the last third, the course overviews interesting
applications of graph embeddings, e.g., the prediction of molecular properties or their use in
combinatorial optimization.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• the current state of the art in machine learning on graphs
• machine learning on graph data and common algorithms
• the theoretical and practical aspects of neural and non-neural methods for graphs
• the limitations of these methods in terms of expressivity and generalization
• typical use cases of machine learning with graphs
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• prove the limitations of machine learning methods for graphs
• implement state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms on graphs
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to

title: Foundations of Learning on Graphs
text:

able to
• assess the limitations of state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms for graphs
• implement state-of-the-art machine learning methods on graphs
• apply theoretical insights from machine learning on graphs to real-world problems

title: Foundations of Learning on Graphs
text: Foundations of Learning on Graphs — prerequisites: Solid Knowledge of Linear Algebra und basic knowledge of graph theory.

title: Research Focus Class on Logic
text:
Research Focus Class on Logic — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): This research-oriented class is is targeted at students who are interested in current problems,
developments and research in the area of logic. This class discusses a selected topic in logic
with special focus on interactive theorem provers like Lean. The class starts with a discussion
of the current state of research in the selected topic. Following every student will pick a specific
question within the selected topic and prepare a presentation to the other participants. Then
the class starts into a phase where students will work out the details of their picked question
and evaluate the results. This phase may also include a study on the ways that artificial
intelligence can help with the picked question. The exact process may change from semester
to semester and depending on the topic.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• the basics of dependent type theory
• how interactive theorem provers like Lean work
• state-of-the art research results on interactive theorem provers
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• research the current scientific results regarding a selected topic
• translate statements from current research ;
• write automated proofs in interactive theorem provers

title: Designing Interactive Systems I
text:
Designing Interactive Systems I — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 1): This class introduces students to human-computer interaction (HCI) and user interface design.
It covers the following topics: Fundamental characteristics of human cognition, such as
reaction time, rules of perception, and memory performance, Models of interaction between
people and their environment, such as affordances, mappings, constraints, slips and mistakes,
Milestones in the history of human-computer interaction, Principles of iterative design, User
interface prototyping techniques, Golden rules of user interface design, User interface design
notations, User studies and evaluation methods.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• how user interfaces have developed over the past decades
• the constants of human performance that need to be considered when designing user
interfaces
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• apply iterative design, prototyping, and evaluation methods to design usable and
appropriate user interfaces in a user-centered fashion
• work in groups to enhance collaboration skills and engage in project-based tasks to
strengthen project planning, conflict management, and presentation skills
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• think in designers’ terms and apply this thinking to real-world problems
• collaborate in interdisciplinary teams to design user interfaces, preparing for future
professional roles

title: Designing Interactive Systems II
text:
Designing Interactive Systems II — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): This module builds on the foundations of Designing Interactive Systems I, and provides
an understanding of how interactive multimedia systems are built from a computer science
point of view. It covers the principles of event-based operating systems, window system
architectures, input and output device technology for multiple modalities, as well as User
Interface Management Systems and UI development toolkits and their relative merits. In the
labs, students will develop a minimalistic window system themselves, but also learn to work
with various real-life development environments, including window systems such as Java
Swing and multimedia development environments, to develop user interfaces.
Knowledge: After successful completion of this module, students know
• how the technology behind interactive systems works
• the architecture of both classic and modern window systems
Skills: After successful completion of this module, students will be able to
• analyze, design, and implement graphical and other user interfaces for existing and
emerging technologies, both for desktop systems and beyond, including interfaces for
multimedia content
• gain hands-on experience in building user interfaces through group-based, project-
centered assignments and lab activities
• foster project management and teamwork skills
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in this module, students will be
able to
• make informed decisions when implementing or managing UI design projects in

industry

title: iOS Application Development
text:
iOS Application Development — content and learning objectives: In this class you learn how to develop mobile application on iOS devices. It covers the
following topics: Introduction of the programming language Swift, Xcode, Storyboards,
Model-View-Controller for iOS, App Frameworks (e.g. UiKit, Foundation), Debugging with
Instruments, Basis iOS Development Frameworks (e.g. MapKit, CoreData, Core Location), iOS
Graphics and Games Frameworks (e.g. Sprite Kit, Scene Kit), Publish Apps in the AppStore.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• the structure of a modern SDK for mobile applications
• the design guidelines for mobile applications
• key software architecture concepts commonly used in the iOS SDK
• the differences between mobile and desktop computing
• an overview of the frameworks provided by the iOS SDK
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• effectively implement their own iOS apps
• use the iOS development environment in depth
• apply an iterative software development process
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• communicate and work in a team
• apply the design guidelines to a specific application scenario
• set up a development plan for a defined application and convincingly present their
results

title: Current Topics in Media Computing and HCI
text:
Current Topics in Media Computing and HCI — content and learning objectives: This class covers current research trends in Human-Computer Interaction and Media
Computing. We use a mix of recent book chapters and papers from conferences and journals
of the last few years to give you an idea of the hot topics that are being worked on in the
international research community. Examples from past years include zoomable user interfaces,
haptic input/output devices, matrix calculus for user interface modelling, and ubiquitous display
technologies.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• how research projects in the area of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) are
established, conducted, evaluated, published, reviewed, and referenced
• findings and technologies that reflect current trends in HCI research
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• survey the literature for topics in the domain of HCI
• read and derive implications from HCI research publications
• assess and discuss the value of published HCI research for academic and industrial
contexts
• summarize and review research publications
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• communicate according to scientific standards, both orally and in writing

title: Virtual Reality
text:
Virtual Reality — content and learning objectives: This course teaches the basic methods for a simulation of virtual environments and introduces
to Virtual Reality applications in the fields of mechanical engineering, simulation science, and
medicine.
The course comes along with practical presentations and covers the following topics:
• The nature and history of VR
• physiological aspects of 3-D visual perception
• VR-related computer graphics
• stereoscopic projections
• projection and interaction hardware
• VR displays
• motion tracking
• collision detection
• 3D user interfaces
• VR applications in research and industry.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• characteristic features of virtual reality
• basic methods and algorithms in virtual reality
• 3D interaction
• stereoscopic projections
• efficient methods for collision detection
• motion tracking
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• systematically evaluate and compare the quality of VR interfaces
• independently design VR interfaces and applications
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• analyze and assess the potentials, challenges, and limitations of VR technologies
• apply learned techniques and methods of virtual reality to new problems

title: CSCW and Groupware: Concepts and Systems for Computer Supported Cooperative Work
text:
CSCW and Groupware: Concepts and Systems for Computer Supported Cooperative Work — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 1): Groupware or CSCW (Computer Supported Cooperative Work) is subject of computer
science and other disciplines to support cooperative work of working groups. Current research
streams focus the integration of groupware, multi media and telecommunication- and internet
services. The lecture presents main concepts and systems of synchronous and asynchronous
communication support (e.g. video conferencing, media spaces, and shared workspaces).
In addition, the lecture treats cooperation support by workflow-management systems and
current trends (CommunityWare, Collaborative Virtual Environments). A special focus is the
presentation and discussion of Blockchain technologies and their application in cooperation
network.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• Concepts, methods and theories of Computer-Supported Cooperative Work (CSCW)
• Functionalities and properties of various cooperation support applications
• Fundamentals of blockchain technology
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• Model cooperation systems
• Analyze requirements for cooperation solutions
• Select appropriate cooperation technologies
• Evaluate blockchain technologies
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• Analyze and assess cooperation systems and architectures, including their
requirements
• Evaluate blockchain solutions and their suitability for different application scenarios

title: Learning Technologies
text:
Learning Technologies — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 4): Learning Technologies research and engineering is an interdisciplinary field involving
competences from cognitive psychology, pedagogy, and various areas within applied computer
science. The course consists of two parts: Theoretical foundations about learning and learning
technologies, and practical approaches for implementing measures, tools, and techniques
related to the theoretical foundations which explore new approaches and develop new
learning technologies and methodologies. The theoretical foundations of the course introduces
learning theories and their implications to eLearning content and system design. These
learning theories are further extended with instructional design theories and multimedia
learning theories about motivation and practical principles which are used as foundations
for designing eLearning content and describe the eLearning design process. Further topics
that are covered in the theoretical foundations include the foundations of assessment and
feedback technologies as well as multimedia tools which support the various aspects of the
teaching and learning processes in education. The first part of the lecture can be conveyed to
the students also by using contemporary e-learning tools and techniques (which include, but
not limited to: video based learning, bMOOCS, flipped classroom methodology) The practical
part of the lecture takes a look at the current learning technologies and tools present in the

title: Learning Technologies
text:
Learning Technologies — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 4): part of the lecture takes a look at the current learning technologies and tools present in the
current learning processes (but not limited to the learning context), and provides a hands-
on approach on building learning technologies tools. The focus is to provide the students a
possibility to gain knowledge and build practical skills for innovating and prototyping learning
tools, services and systems which can be used in different educational contexts. The practical
work and approaches will be connected with new learning theories and approaches which
better address the new challenges which come up with the processes for digitalizing the
learning environments and the new digital environments within the learning processes.. The
course will introduce novel technologies for implementing innovative learning systems and
components for open networked learning, and will also include techniques, methodologies
and approaches which handle data, data analysis, data literacy and similar novel concepts
which arise from using technology within education. The assignments take the form of practical
lab courses with mandatory attendance. In the mandatory attendance sessions, the students
will do hands-on exercises and receive guidelines, suggestions, and tips about designing and
implementing learning tools. As an example, a typical task consists of starting with an idea
about tool/component/system, and then iteratively develop it in a finished product, applying

title: Learning Technologies
text:
Learning Technologies — content and learning objectives (part 3 of 4): about tool/component/system, and then iteratively develop it in a finished product, applying
agile practical techniques, modern software engineering tools and technologies by following a
(user) learner-centered approach. Students can work on these assignments alone, or in small
teams.
Knowledge: After successful completion of this module, students know
• the main aspects of current learning theories
• a systematic process of eLearning content design
• design principles for multimedia learning and their relation to cognitive psychology and
pedagogy
• how to apply models of cognitive psychology and instructional design theories in
eLearning projects
• taxonomies of learning objectives and provide appropriate examples
• reasons for and examples of eTests and automatic feedback

and multimedia learning design principles

implementing Learning Technologies

technology-enhanced learning
• develop ideas and design them as technical solutions in a learning scenario

learning tools and technologies
• possess practical agile software development skills, including managing software

title: Learning Technologies
text:
Learning Technologies — content and learning objectives (part 4 of 4): learning tools and technologies
• possess practical agile software development skills, including managing software
projects and deliverables

designing test items
• apply principles of assessment and feedback design when implementing test sets
• systematically plan, design, and implement small to medium-sized eLearning projects
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in this module, students will be
able to
• scientifically communicate aspects of eLearning design and eLearning research

learning technologies development and application
• work in interdisciplinary teams to design and implement technology-enhanced learning
and propose creative solutions in eLearning projects
• take responsibility in project work as reliable project partners

models.

title: Research Focus Class on Learning Technologies
text:
Research Focus Class on Learning Technologies — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): This research-oriented course is aimed at students who are interested in current issues,
developments and research in the field of modern learning technologies. A selected topic
from one of the following areas of learning technologies will be discussed: Learning Analytics,
Learning Games, Mobile Learning, Blended Learning, Computer Science Didactics etc. The
first step will be an introduction to the current state of research in the selected subject area.
In the following, each student should identify a question (research idea) in the subject area
under guidance and familiarise themselves with it and present it to the other participants. This
concept phase is followed by a practical phase in which the students work out their research
idea (prototype implementation, analysis, simulation, etc.) and evaluate it. The exact procedure
can vary from semester to semester and depending on the subject area.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• basic current research topics in the field of learning technologies and/or computer
science education
• basic web technologies and their application for technology-supported teaching and
learning
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• apply scientific methods to develop their own results both theoretically and practically
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• work in depth on a selected, current topic

title: Research Focus Class in Computer Science Education
text:
Research Focus Class in Computer Science Education — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): This research-oriented course is aimed at students who want to deal with current
developments, questions and research approaches in the field of computer science didactics
and modern learning technologies. The course deals with a selected topic from one of the
following areas: Computer Science Didactics, VR Learning Simulations, Learning Analytics or
related topics.
At the beginning, students receive an introduction to the current state of research in the
chosen subject area. They then identify their own research question under supervision and
systematically work their way into the topic. They present their findings to the group and reflect
on the implications for computer science education and technology-supported teaching and
learning in various situations, e.g. in school, extracurricular learning venues or teacher training.
In the subsequent practical phase, students deepen their research idea through further
analysis or prototypical implementation, for example by developing a concept, implementation
or an empirical study. They use scientific methods for the structured development of their own
results.
The exact procedure may vary depending on the semester and subject area (see https://
www.ddi.rwth-aachen.de/cms/ddi/Studium/Lehrveranstaltungen/~bmfmih/RFC/).
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• basic didactic principles for computer science education
• relevant aspects of teacher professionalization for (prospective) computer science

title: Research Focus Class in Computer Science Education
text:
Research Focus Class in Computer Science Education — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): • basic didactic principles for computer science education
• relevant aspects of teacher professionalization for (prospective) computer science
teachers
• basic research topics in the fields of learning technologies and/or computer science
education
• basic technologies for the education sector and their potential uses for technology-
supported teaching and learning

education with a focus on teacher interaction
• analyze and discuss potential impacts of specific teacher interactions on the course of
a lesson

• apply scientific methods for generating their own results both theoretically and
practically

able to

challenging computer science teaching-learning scenarios in the form of structured
decision trees
• deepen their knowledge of a selected, current research topic and acquire the ability to
independently familiarize themselves with scientific issues

title: Mobile Internet Technology
text:
Mobile Internet Technology — content and learning objectives: This course addresses architectures, protocols, and algorithms for mobile Internet systems:
• Physical layer: modulation, coding and signal propagation
• MAC layer: challenges in wireless medium access
• Wireless, data-oriented networks: 802.11 (WLAN)
• Routing in Ad-hoc networks
• Mobile networks: GSM, GPRS, UMTS, LTE, 5G
• Mobility in the Internet: Mobile IP, HIP, TCP
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• the basic principles of wireless networks, specifically 802.11 (WLAN) and mobile
networks
• the issues related to Internet protocols (IP, TCP) in mobile scenarios
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• identify and solve problems in mobile scenarios
• recognize common aspects of various wireless network solutions
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• methodically analyze the applicability of wireless mobile system architectures to future
Internet scenarios
• discuss the requirements for Internet protocols in wireless mobile systems and develop
solutions to meet these requirements

title: Mobile Internet Technology
text:
Mobile Internet Technology — prerequisites: Basic knowledge in data communication, e.g. lecture 'Data Communication and Internet
Technology' & Contents of the lecture "Secure Distributed Systems". Students must pass the

Basic knowledge in data communication is recommended

title: Advanced Internet Technology
text:
Advanced Internet Technology — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 1): Introductory courses in communication systems deal with the classic communication principles
of the Internet. These communication techniques are still in use, but are not able to cope with
all the requirements of modern networks. This course gives an introduction into advanced
communication paradigms that build upon the existing Internet technology:
• Realizing scalable applications and communication: Peer-to-Peer systems and Cloud
Computing
• Integration of devices with restricted resources into the Internet: Cyber-physical
Systems and the Internet of Things
• Realization of adaptive communication: Software Defined Networking and Quality of
Service
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• restrictions of classical communication principles in the modern Internet
• basic principles for realizing scalable, adaptive and resource constraint communication
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• identify sources of problems of classical communication protocols in modern
communication systems
• apply algorithms for scalable, adaptive and resource constraint communication
Competences: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• analyze the applicability of solutions for scalable, adaptive and resource constraint
communication to future mobile Internet scenarios methodically
• identify possibilities of evolving modern communication systems

text:

Ditributed Systems) sind hilfreich.

title: Communication Systems Engineering
text:
Communication Systems Engineering — content and learning objectives: This lecture addresses the foundations and technologies required in the engineering of modern
communication systems:
• Protocol Design: basic methods for designing communication protocols
• Implementation: tools and technologies for implementing communication systems in
both kernel space and user space

implementation

able to
• design novel communication systems and evaluate their performance

title: Embedded Systems
text:
Embedded Systems — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Embedded systems control many things in our daily life. Energy-efficient refrigerators, elevator
controls, and advanced driver assistance systems are just some examples. Embedded
systems also control processes in industrial environments and are used to detect and prevent
system failures. This lecture gives a general introduction to the topic of embedded systems.
It introduces basic concepts and points out important differences to “normal” computer
systems. This lecture prepares students for advanced lectures of the Embedded Software
Laboratory that cover safety, reliability, formal methods and dynamic systems in detail. This
lecture is targeted at all students that do not want to limit themselves to understanding PCs
but also want to know how, for example, engine control units and production control systems
work. Topics covered in this lecture are: Microcontroller, Programmable logic controllers
(PLCs, PLC programming languages, Real-time requirements, Real-time operating systems,
Characteristics of embedded software design, Intra vehicle communication (e.g., CAN bus),
Teasers of advanced lectures of the embedded software laboratory, The lecture will be held in
German with English slides.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• modern software techniques for embedded systems
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• apply a model-based, quality-oriented approach to the design of embedded software

title: Embedded Systems
text:
Embedded Systems — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): • apply a model-based, quality-oriented approach to the design of embedded software
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• identify and appropriately address specific qualitative requirements in the design of
embedded software

title: Functional Safety and System Dependability
text:
Functional Safety and System Dependability — content and learning objectives: • Basic terms (damage, risik, safety, reliability, availability, etc.)
• Reference model reliability (error prevention vs. Fault tolerance, defect-
faultbreakdown)
• Design patterns for reliability (Redundancy, Replication)
• Analysis methods for Reliability (RBDs, fault trees)

Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• the terminology, criteria and analysis and design methods for safety- and reliability-
related systems
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to

• verify these requirements
• take them into account when designing such systems
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• develop a sensitivity to safety- and reliability-related design issues and address them
appropriately

title: Formal Methods for Logic Control Software
text:
Formal Methods for Logic Control Software — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): This Lecture represents an application-oriented Introduction to various formal methods. The
lecture focuses on the Application of formal methods during the design process of logic control
software. The lecture comprises the following topics:

• Abstract Interpretation
• Program Slicing

• challenges in the analysis of control software
• techniques and formalisms for static analysis

• modelling of PLC programs for verification
• various techniques for specifying system requirements
• methods for verifying different specifications
• techniques for encoding PLC semantics as formulas for SMT solvers
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• build a framework for static analysis
• derive program properties by selecting appropriate abstract domains for static analysis
• perform dependency analysis and simplify programs through program slicing
• encode PLC programs as formulas for satisfiability checking with SMT solvers
• design requirement specifications using appropriate formalisms
• verify specifications using suitable model-checking algorithms
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to

title: Advanced Microcontroller Programming and Debugging
text:
Advanced Microcontroller Programming and Debugging — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): The course aims to provide a comprehensive overview of methods for programming of
microcontrollers and the debugging, respectively. There will be covered different programming
techniques, backgrounds about the software development tool-chains best practices about the
programming of microcontrollers and different techniques of de-bugging as deep as performing
measurements at the copper layer.
The course will dive deeper into the following topics:
• Practical aspects of the compiler tool-chain
• Programming language C
• Coding guidelines
• Runtime behavior
• Debugging at the copper layer
• Protective Circuits
• First embedded insights to model-based software development and testing
The above will be complemented with hands-on assignments using various examples (still to
be determined).
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know

• the structure and composition of embedded systems
• the interaction between the microcontroller and the embedded environment
• common sources of errors in microcontroller programming and methods for
troubleshooting
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• program a microcontroller in an embedded environment
• understand and apply the interaction between the microcontroller and the embedded
environment
• identify, analyze, and effectively debug malfunctions

title: Advanced Microcontroller Programming and Debugging
text:
Advanced Microcontroller Programming and Debugging — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): environment
• identify, analyze, and effectively debug malfunctions

able to

• diagnose and fix issues in embedded systems

title: Digitalisation
text:
Digitalisation — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): The lecture “Digitalisation” examines the topic of digitalization from different perspectives and
angles: The basics of the term digitization and its classification in the discipline are taught.
Discussions will encourage a critical examination of the term. Lecturers from the business
world deal with current developments that are advancing the digitalization of their economic
sector. In a written assignment, the presentation on two areas is summarized and compared,
supplemented with current literature and reflected on in relation to the student's own future
career.
Knowledge: After successful completion of this module, students know
• the concept of digitization and its classification within the field of study
• practical application areas of digitization
• current developments in digitization within various industries as presented by guest
speakers
Skills: After successful completion of this module, students will be able to
• critically engage with the topic of digitization from different perspectives
• summarize and compare presentations on digitization, complement them with current
literature, and reflect on them in relation to their future careers
• identify the role of digitization in their own professional field
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in this module, students will be
able to
• reflect on the implications of digitization for their own career and professional
development

title: Digitalisation
text:
Digitalisation — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): able to

title: Research Focus Class on Communication Systems
text:
Research Focus Class on Communication Systems — content and learning objectives: This research-oriented course addresses students with an interest in current Internet
technology research and development. A selected topic from the following areas of
communication systems will be discussed:
• Network architectures
• Cyber-physical systems
• Security and privacy
• Systems analysis.
The course starts with an overview on the state of the art in the selected subject area. Basing
on this introductory part, the students identify specific research topics (guided by the teaching
assistants) for scientific examination of certain aspects. Each student presents a topic with
focus on research questions. In the second part of the course the students work on their topic
practically (prototypical implementation, simulations, analysis, ...). The concrete outline might
vary from semester to semester, depending on the topical area.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• detailed current research topics in the field of communication systems and distributed
systems
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• apply scientific methods for developing their own theoretical and practical results
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• conduct an in-depth study of a selected current topic
• independently explore a research topic

title: Research Focus Class on Communication Systems

title: Industrial Network Security
text:
Industrial Network Security — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): This course provides an introduction into current security problems of industrial networks and
state-of-the-art security solutions. After an introduction into industrial networks and protocols
and their prevalent security issues, students will learn about approaches to prevent and detect
as well as react to cyberattacks and security incidents. Topics include security approaches
for legacy industrial control systems with tight resource-constraints, security assessments of
industrial networks, and intrusion detection and prevention in future industrial networks.
This course will provide students with an understanding of the unique challenges of realizing
security within industrial networks and provide them with the necessary conceptual tools to
properly secure industrial networks.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• the specific security challenges of industrial networks
• the technical constraints that distinguish industrial networks from traditional IT
networks
• approaches for preventing, detecting and responding to advanced cyberattacks on
industrial networks
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• select and apply conceptual tools for the comprehensive security of industrial networks
• assess scenario-specific constraints and derive suitable security measures
• prioritize the deployment of applicable security mechanisms based on context

title: Industrial Network Security
text:
Industrial Network Security — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): • prioritize the deployment of applicable security mechanisms based on context
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• identify and analyze prevalent security issues in industrial networks across different
domains
• evaluate the applicability of standard IT security methods to industrial settings
• determine when and how dedicated security approaches must be applied for effective
protection

title: Industrial Network Security

title: Control and Perception in Networked and Autonomous Vehicles
text:
Control and Perception in Networked and Autonomous Vehicles — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): This course combines theory of multi-agent decision-making with practical exercises in
the Cyber-Physical Mobility Lab (CPM Lab, an open source platform for networked and
autonomous vehicles). In the theory part, we focus on distributing the control problem of multi-
agent systems coupled via objective function or constraints using Distributed MPC (DMPC).
Additionally, the course discusses the application in a multi-vehicle system, which prepares the
participants for the practical lab work. In the CPM Lab, the students implement controllers for
vehicle platoons.
The course covers the following topics
1. Vehicle models: mass-point, kinematic, and kinetic.
2. Control engineering and optimization: model predictive control, convex optimization,
non-convex optimization.
3. Network and distribution: graph theory, distributed algorithms, cooperative and non-
cooperative approaches to networked control.
4. Machine perception: neural networks.
5. Software architectures and testing concepts: service-oriented software architecture, In-
the-loop testing concepts for networked systems.
6. Case study: vehicle platoon.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• methods for developing control and perception algorithms in connected and
autonomous vehicles
• subject areas relevant for the implementation of control and perception algorithms
• procedures for modeling, control, optimization, perception, distribution, as well as
design and testing in such vehicles

title: Control and Perception in Networked and Autonomous Vehicles
text:
Control and Perception in Networked and Autonomous Vehicles — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): • procedures for modeling, control, optimization, perception, distribution, as well as
design and testing in such vehicles
• challenges of real-time capable implementation of algorithms
• approaches and process models for algorithm development and their advantages and
disadvantages
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• independently perform the steps necessary to develop control and perception
algorithms
• evaluate and apply available approaches, methods, and algorithms appropriately
• synthesize control and perception algorithms

Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to

algorithms in connected and autonomous vehicles
• select and apply suitable procedures and evaluate their applicability in specific
scenarios
• develop application-oriented solutions considering real-time constraints and validate
them experimentally

title: IT-Security 1 - Cryptographic Basics and Network Security
text:
IT-Security 1 - Cryptographic Basics and Network Security — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): The lecture consists of two parts. The first part covers the cryptographic basics including:
Symmetric Encryption, Integrity protection, Asymmetric Encryption, Digital Signatures,
Certificates and Public Key Infrastructures, and Authentication and Key Agreement. The
second part is dedicated to Network Security including Kerberos, IPsec, TLS protocol, SSH,
DNS Security, Email Security, and Phishing Attacks.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• the cryptographic primitives symmetric / asymmetric encryption, digital signatures,
cryptographic hash function, and message authentication codes
• the security features offered by the latest versions of the most important security
protocols operating on the TCP/IP stack including IPsec, TLS, SSH, DNSsec, and
PGP
• known attacks against these security protocols
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• select and apply appropriate cryptographic primitives in different application scenarios
• select suitable security protocols for a given scenario and configure the relevant
options for the cryptographic building blocks used within these protocols
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• identify security requirements and adequate security mechanisms in various
application domains
• identify potential weaknesses in security protocols not covered in detail during the
course and propose appropriate fixes

text:

• identify potential weaknesses in security protocols not covered in detail during the

primitives

title: IT-Security 2 - Computer Security
text:

on system security. The second part of the lecture is dedicated to privacy in applications.
The first part includes: Malware, Buffer Overflows and other Memory Corruptions, Denial of
Service Attacks, Access Control, Firewalls, and Intrusion Detection. The second part includes:
Anonymous Communications, Electronic Payment, Biometrics, Electronic Voting, and Secure
Multi-Party Computation.

• the components of biometric systems and the security and privacy implications of
different biometric applications
• how electronic payment methods function
• the challenges of electronic voting systems
• different electronic voting systems and attacks against them
• the challenges of anonymous communications and how different anonymous
communication networks operate
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• identify and fix buffer overflows and other memory corruptions in code
• apply and configure firewalls
• apply the Tor protocol

title: Advanced Network Security
text:
Advanced Network Security — content and learning objectives: In this module we study cryptographic protocols and security architectures of wireless as well
as wired networks. We will focus on cryptographic and design weaknesses and study well-
known attacks against them. We will cover the architectures of and attacks against mobile
telecommunication networks, WLAN, Bluetooth, EAP and EAP-Methods, BGP, FIDO2 as well
as already known protocols such as TLS.

• the security architectures of common communication networks
• typical design weaknesses and attacks targeting security architectures and protocols
• solution approaches for mitigating these vulnerabilities

title: Advanced Operating Systems
text:
Advanced Operating Systems — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): In this course, we will study in details the design and implementation of a full, modern
operating system: xv6. This operating system was developed at MIT, and is a re-
implementation of the original Unix v6 operating system. It is a small and simple operating
system implemented for the RISC-V architecture, which is easy to understand and modify.
Compared to full-fledged operating systems like Linux, xv6 is much smaller and simpler, which
makes it a great tool for learning about operating systems.
We will cover all operating systems components: virtual memory, file systems, threading,
interrupts, IPCs, etc. The lectures will cover the core architecture and concepts of xv6, as well
as more general operating systems concerns. We will also study the implementation of these
components in xv6, and how to extend them. During the labs, you will modify the xv6 code
base to implement new features, and you will be evaluated on your implementation.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• fundamental concepts of operating systems, including:
• memory management techniques such as paging
• thread and process management
• device driver fundamentals
• file system structures
• synchronization mechanisms
• interactions between user space and kernel space
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• read and understand C code in the context of an operating system kernel

title: Advanced Operating Systems
text:
Advanced Operating Systems — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• read and understand C code in the context of an operating system kernel
• modify and extend the xv6 operating system to implement new functionality or improve
existing components
• debug and resolve issues in both kernel code and user-space applications
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• analyze and troubleshoot operating system behavior and performance problems
• design appropriate solutions to technical challenges in OS development
• adapt operating system concepts and source code to new scenarios or requirements

title: Real-Time Systems and Applications
text:
Real-Time Systems and Applications — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 1): Real-time systems play a crucial role in many modern applications and systems, especially
when data processing units need to be integrated into physical systems. This module provides
both fundamental and advanced knowledge of real-time systems themselves and their
applications. The lectures in this module cover the design and analysis necessary to ensure
compliance with the requirements for real-time systems. This knowledge is reinforced and
applied in practice during the exercises. The module is particularly suitable for students
interested in research related to cyber-physical systems and embedded systems.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• fundamental concepts for the design and analysis of real-time systems
• principles of worst-case analysis in real-time systems
• current methods for verifying the schedulability of real-time systems
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• perform worst-case analyses for real-time systems
• apply current methods to verify the schedulability of real-time systems

Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to

title: Real-Time Operating Systems - Design and Implementation
text:
Real-Time Operating Systems - Design and Implementation — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 1): Real-time operating systems have to serve as the backbone of many modern real-time
systems. Compared to standard operating systems, they have to fulfill different targets and
need to implement fundamentally different concepts. This lecture covers two directions. On
the one hand, this lecture will teach the differences between standard operating systems and
real-time operating systems. On the other hand, this lecture will teach the fundamental design
concept of real-time operating systems by letting students implement parts of a real-time
operating system on their own.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• basic routines of operating systems (such as interrupt handling and context switch)
• real-time operating system specific routines (timer tick, queues)
• advanced real-time operating system concepts (schedulers, servers)
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• implement basic routines of operating systems
• implement specific routines of real-time operating systems
• use existing real-time operating systems
Competencies: Based on the knowledge and skills acquired in the module, students will be
able to
• design and analyze real-time operating systems in a structured and methodical way
• evaluate and choose real-time operating systems based on the realized features
• demonstrate and justify the correct use of real-time operating system specific feaures
for real-time applications

title: Implementation of Databases
text:
Implementation of Databases — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): The module discusses the key aspects of the implementation of database systems. This
includes an introduction of basic architectures (e.g. layered architecture) as well the
procedures necessary for solving individual tasks (especially query processing and transaction
management). The concepts of implementation will be applied to classical relational model as
well as to more recent data models (distributed, object-oriented, deductive, search engines).
In addition to the necessary theoretical background practical concepts will be introduced that
allow database administrators the efficient tuning of databases.

• professionally evaluate, administer and tune existing databases

title: Introduction to Data Science
text:
Introduction to Data Science — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 3): The course aims to provide a comprehensive overview of data science and expose students to
real-life data sets and tools. The course provides three angles on data science:
1. Data science infrastructure concerned with volume and velocity. Topics include
instrumentation, big data infrastructures, and distributed systems, databases and data
management, and programming, and the main challenge is to make making things
scalable and instant.
2. Data science analysis concerned with extracting knowledge from data. Topics include
statistics, data|process mining, machine learning|artificial intelligence, operations
research, algorithms, and visualization, and the main challenge is to provide answers
to known and unknown unknowns.
3. Data science effects concerned with people, organizations, and society. Topics include
ethics &; privacy, IT law, human-technology interaction, operations management,
business models, entrepreneurship, and the main challenge is to do all of the above in
a responsible manner.
