title: Advanced Process Mining
text:
Advanced Process Mining — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 4): Process mining provides a new means to improve processes in a variety of application
domains. There are two main drivers for this new technology. On the one hand, more and more
events are being recorded thus providing detailed information about the history of processes.
On the other hand, in most organizations, there is a need to improve process performance
(e.g. to reduce costs and flow time) and compliance (e.g. to avoid deviations or risks). Process
mining bridges the gap between model-based process analyses (e.g., simulation, model
checking, and classical BPM techniques) and data-oriented techniques (e.g. data mining
techniques like classification, clustering, and regression). Process mining techniques can be
applied in a variety of domains. ;
Some examples:
• Discovering the root causes for delays in treatment processes in a hospital: What
groups of patients are not treated according to the guidelines?
• Diagnosing the behaviour of an X-ray machine that malfunctions and suggesting
preventative maintenance: What component should be replaced?
• Analysing the "customer journey" of customers that have purchased a product and
are using related services: How to seduce customers to purchase more services and
additional products?
• Checking the conformance of processes in local governments to find potential cases of
fraud: Why was the formal approval step bypassed frequently?
• Analysing the study behaviour of students following a Massive Open Online Course

text:
Advanced Process Mining — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 4): fraud: Why was the formal approval step bypassed frequently?

students that fail the course?
• Analysing a luggage handling system in an airport to understand where luggage gets
delayed or misplaced: When and why is the baggage handling system not meeting the
service level agreements?
• Discovering the actual processes supported by a service desk of a large bank: Why
does it take such a long time before a person is found that can assist in solving the
problem?

foundations to ultimately address business questions as illustrated above. We will explore
advanced process discovery algorithms based on Petri net synthesis and state-of-the-art
alignment-based conformance checking, including implementation aspects. Additionally,
you will be introduced to novel research directions in process mining, such as object-centric
process mining and the unique challenges it presents.
Moreover, you will further deepen your understanding by applying these concepts in a written
homework assignment, gaining practical experience with process mining tools and challenges.

• the entire spectrum of process mining and how process mining techniques relate

text:
Reinforcement Learning and Learning-based Control — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Class outline:
• Reinforcement learning problem and its relation to control

• Reinforcement learning with function approximation incl. deep RL

Wissen und Verstehen:
The course “Reinforcement Learning and Learning-based Control” covers fundamentals and
state-of-the art methods in reinforcement learning and learning-based control. Reinforcement
learning (RL) is a machine learning paradigm that aims at learning action or control policies
from data generated through interaction with an environment. It is one important subfield of
learning-based control (LBC), which more broadly denotes the intersection of the areas of
automatic control and machine learning. Both, RL and LBC are very active and interdisciplinary
areas of research.
The first part of the module introduces and formalizes the reinforcement learning problem and
its connections with dynamical systems and control. Building on the formulation as a Markov
decision process, core concepts of RL and optimal control will be developed. After establishing
understanding and fundamental concepts of RL theory, modern algorithms including deep RL
approaches are introduced. In addition to RL, the course covers further essential topics of
learning-based control, including model learning and modern controller tuning techniques

title: Stochastic Processes and Dynamical Systems
text:
Stochastic Processes and Dynamical Systems — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): A wide range of real-world phenomena are subject to dynamical movement, change, and
dependency on their past. This behavior is particularly prominent in engineering and computer
systems. In particular, when additional stochastic effects are influencing the dynamics, it
is necessary to generalize standard concepts from probabilty theory through an explicit
time component. This class aims at conveying a measure theoretical introduction to these
advanced topics and we start we introducing conditional expected values with respect to
sigma algebras. This a very general formulation and critical for considering processes that are
defined in continuous time and general state spaces. We will consider Markov processes that
go beyond the often considered discrete state-space and discrete time Markov chains. Further,
we investigate selected special cases such as the famoues Wiener process and some of its
properties. We will generalize to the Ohrnstein-Uhlenbeck process and touch upon stochastic
differential equations. Stochastic processes and dynamical systems are key concepts in theory
and practice. This class covers some of the mathematical foundations for further research-
oriented topics that consider a data-driven approach to treating stochastic processes and
dynamical systems.
Knowledge and Understanding:
This class is mathematically oriented and we consider stochastic processes and dynamical

title: Stochastic Processes and Dynamical Systems
text:
Stochastic Processes and Dynamical Systems — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): dynamical systems.
Knowledge and Understanding:
This class is mathematically oriented and we consider stochastic processes and dynamical
systems from a measure theoratical point of view. Both are fundamental for modeling various
modern systems in engineering and computer science. In essence, they describe the evolution
of systems that depend on their own past. The mathematical analysis of these systems allows
to predict, analyze and control them. Depending on the application, there can be stochastic or
determinsitc behavior.
Skills and Competencies:
The key objective is to convey the key ideas and concepts, while also proving and discussing
selected results in more detail. The obtained insights are tailored to improve the understanding
of stochastic processes from a measure theoretical perspective. Here, we will also focus
on standard results and insights. We will cover the special case of linear and time-invariant
systems in great detail due to the analytical tractability. The deterministic case will receive
special attention for its relevance in modern control theory. Among others, we will cover
conditional expected values and Markow processes in various settings (descrete time,
continuous time, finite state spaces), where we discuss selected examples such as the
Brownian Motion and Ornstein Ulhenbeck process alongside their properties.

title: Social and Technological Change
text:
Social and Technological Change — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): The course is devoted to unpack basic questions like: How to make technology work for us?
Has it worked for us in the past? Will it work for us in the future? Is there a monolithic "us"?
What is actually what we want, collectively and individually? How do we act, collectively and
individually? We cannot answer these questions without knowing some history, economics,
politics, psychology, and evolutionary biology. In the course, we will make such a tour, and
in parts, we will draw on bits of probability, causality, and game theory, to sharpen our critical
thinking skills.
Some of the topics to be covered in the lectures include:
• Understanding the current situation: risk and possibilities
• History, progress, technology
• Industrial revolution and capitalism
• Market and morals
• The ascent of reason, the Enlightenment
• The limits of reason: where goals come from (evolution), dilemmas of collective action
(game theory)
• The limits of reason 2 : culture, evolution, social emotions
• AI: risks and opportunities
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• the social context of technological development in the past and present
• the economic context of technological development in the past and present
• the historical context of technological development in the past and present
• the ethical context of technological development in the past and present
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to

title: Advanced Topics in Machine Learning for Human Language Technology
text:
Advanced Topics in Machine Learning for Human Language Technology — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Today data-driven methods like machine learning and artificial neural networks (ANN) are
widely used for speech and language processing, e.g. for automatic speech recognition (ASR)
and machine translation. We will re-visit the evolution of these methods over the last 50 years
and will present a unifying view of their principles from a probabilistic perspective.
• Part 1: Probabilistic foundations, Bayes decision theory, probabilistic interpretation of
neural networks, training criteria.
• Part 2: Sequence processing and specific ANN structures (hidden markov models,
finite-state transducers, cross-attention).
• Part 3: Deep Learning and HLT tasks (automatic speech recognition, language
modelling, machine translation).
Knowledge: ;After successful completion of the module, students know
• the components and formalisms of machine learning problems in human language
technology from a principled probabilistic perspective
• optimization problems of machine learning for human language technology and its
relation to performance evaluation
Skills: ;After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• apply state-of-the-art machine learning models to human language technology
components
• solve the optimization problems underlying decoding in sequence classification based
on state-of-the-art machine learning components and underlying models
• should have acquired soft skills like acquiring, reproducing and discussing knowledge

title: Research Focus Class on Data Ecosystems
text:

title: Introduction to Program Synthesis
text:
Introduction to Program Synthesis — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): The lecture "Introduction to Program Synthesis" covers its historical background, fundamentals
and state-of-the-art methods used for program synthesis. It first sketches the historical
background of computer programs and program synthesis, introduces the most fundamental
dogmas prevalent in program synthesis, and covers the core basics of machine learning
and optimization. The lecture then focuses on the fundamental understanding of basic
(traditional) methods and concepts that have been proposed over time. The last part of the
lecture addresses modern techniques that are based on contemporary machine learning and
optimization concepts and are used for state-of-the-art applications.
The scope of the lecture therefore combines a fundamental and formal understanding of
computer programs in general, basic and traditional concepts that have been used in program
synthesis, as well as modern (state-of-the-art) methods.
Lecture outline:
1. Fundamentals of computer programs (history, definition and representation)
2. General principles of program synthesis (paradigms and search spaces)
3. Traditional concepts (enumerative, inductive/deductive, and stochastic search)
4. Machine-learning methods (Neural Program Synthesis, Genetic Programming, GenAI/
LLMs)
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module students know
• Formal definition and fundamental design as well as representations of computer
programs, traditional and modern principles and techniques in program synthesis

title: Industrial Data Security
text:
Industrial Data Security — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): This course provides an introduction into current security problems surrounding industrial data
and state-of-the-art security solutions. After an introduction into industrial data, how it is stored
and processes, as well as prevalent security issues surrounding industrial data, students
will learn about approaches to secure industrial data across files, databases, and machine
learning. Topics include encryption and integrity-protection of structured industrial data in files,
database security in industrial contexts, as well as machine learning security for industrial
data. Across all topics, a special emphasis will be put on the privacy-preserving processing of
industrial data.
This course will provide students with an understanding of the unique challenges of securely
operating on industrial data and provide them with the necessary conceptual tools to properly
secure industrial data.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• the unique security challenges of industrial data compared to other domains
• approaches to securing industrial data across files, databases and machine learning
applications
• fundamental concepts and principles for securing industrial data
Skills: After successful completion of the module, students will be able to
• select and apply suitable conceptual tools to ensure the security of industrial data
• assess the constraints of a given industrial scenario and prioritize applicable security
measures

title: Artificial Intelligence in Music
text:
Artificial Intelligence in Music — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): The goal of this course is to provide an introduction into the research field Artificial Intelligence
(AI) in music using traditional and modern algorithms, including music information retrieval
(MIR) and machine learning (ML) approaches: basics of digital music processing, extraction
of various features from audio, score, and other music related data, classification scenarios,
music generation and algorithm evaluation, etc.
The course is organised into four segments:
1. Foundations: backgrounds of music data processing and analysis of different
modalities (audio, score, text, images, social data, etc.)
2. Mid-Level Features: application of supervised classification to predict semantically
meaningful descriptors of music pieces
3. High-Level Categories: methods to organise music collections (e.g., based on genres
or emotions), recommendation systems, user friendly evaluation
4. Music Generation: from rule-based systems to text-to-music models
Another key component of this course is the critical evaluation of AI methods for music
related applications from different perspectives including classification quality, interpretability,
robustness, and resources.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the course, students will know:
• the backgrounds of AI in music
• scenarios how AI can be applied to analyse and generate musical data
• multi-objective evaluation of related methods
Skills: After successful completion of the course, students will be able to

title: Web3 & Distributed Ledger Technology
text:

blockchain technologies. Blockchain is considered as one specific instance of Distributed

management across flexible business partnerships.
• Foundations – Distributed transaction management versus centralized databases with
their ACID properties for consistency management will be discussed first. Then, DLT
will be introduced as enabler of the Internet of Value as guarantor of ledgers for asset
management as well as micro transactions unveiling new spheres of businesses.
• Core technologies – Enabling technologies to establish new process patterns for
the collaboration of businesses to enabler virtual enterprises and other enterprise
innovations; enabling technologies include hashing, perception hashes, Merkle trees
for the representation of transactions, consensus for process synchronization as well
as tokens &;;; ;;;tokenization for business modelling.
• Use case portfolio – A selection of typical uses cases to illustrate the application
spectrum of DLT. A spectrum of use case scenarios will be presented ranging from
production industries via identity management towards self-sovereign organizational
structures and their governance structure.

title: Knowledge Graphs
text:
Knowledge Graphs — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Knowledge Graphs represent knowledge as a network of entities and their relationships and
form the basis of many modern data-driven applications. As part of the W3C Semantic Web
initiative, standards and technologies have been developed for machine-readable exchange
of data, information and knowledge on the Web, which to this day provide the technical
foundation of open Knowledge Graphs. These standards and technologies are increasingly
being used in applications and have already led to a number of exciting projects (e.g. DBpedia,
Wikidata, semantic wikis, or commercial applications such as schema.org, OpenCalais, or
Google's Knowledge Graph). Increasingly, Knowledge Graphs also serve as a foundation for
generative AI: they supply large language models with reliable, structured factual knowledge
and thus enable traceable answers. Approaches such as graph-based retrieval-augmented
generation (GraphRAG) combine the expressive power of language models with the precision
and verifiability of symbolic knowledge representation. The module provides a theoretically

title: Software Language Engineering
text:
Software Language Engineering — content and learning objectives: "The limits of my language are the limits of my world." Ludwig Wittgenstein. This is all the more
true when people communicate with computers.
The course deals with concepts of language definition, such as meta-models, grammars,
modern editors and the use of software languages, for example for modeling software,
systems, and simulations. It discusses examples such as UML, domain-specific languages
(DSL) and XML, as well as semantic analysis and generation techniques.
DSLs are always useful and often necessary where non-computer scientists have to deal with
computers and have to model complex facts, scenarios or systems. DSL models are suited for
modelling the human brain, automous cars, E-home components. They allow to generate code
or orchestrate business processes in the cloud, and much more.

text:
High-performance Matrix Computations — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): The course centers around the idea of developing efficient numerical algorithms for matrix

eigenproblems, matrix factorizations, linear systems. The students are expected to participate

title: Software Architecture
text:
Software Architecture — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 3): In this module we investigate modern software architecures from different perspectives and
viewpoints. We discuss architectural decision making, recording and trade-off discussions
based on relevant requirements—a theme that pervades the entire lecture. We investigate
different architectural patterns and styles of modern software architectures with emphasis
on event-driven microservices. Domain-driven design (DDD) is introduced and applied to
develop the insides of a service following principles of clean and hexagonal architectures.
From developing one service, we then move on to more distributed settings where strategic
DDD patterns come into play and we discuss service granularities and service cutting. In
these distributed settings, we investigate different aspects that are architecturally relevant
for interactions between services: communication styles, messaging and events, data
persistence and ownership, consistency, and distributed transactions. In this context we
introduce workflow systems for service orchestration. Once the software system is developed,
we start investigating its performance and resilience. We test the system, attack it, and
introduce resilience patterns to cope with failures. In the last part of the lecture, we focus
on the modeling and analysis of architectures, and investigate domain-specific software
architectures. The use of AI in the context of software architectures will also be discussed. In

text:

the exercise, we incrementally develop a complex software system in groups where we apply
the concepts from the lecture and will use modern tools, frameworks, and systems ;that are
widely used in industry.
Knowledge: After successful completion of the module, students know
• Design principles and patterns for modern software architectures
• Challenges and trade-offs in designing and developing architectures of distributed
software systems

the architecture level

and principles (tactical domain-driven design)

title: Biotechnology (In Depth Module)
text:
Biotechnology (In Depth Module) — content and learning objectives (part 3 of 4): • 13.8 FhuA-Toolbox
Wissen und Verstehen:
Durch die Vorlesung "Reaktionstechnik" wird das Verständnis für grundlegende Phänomene
der Reaktionskinetik vermittelt. Die Studierenden kennen den Einfluss kinetischer Größen auf
chemische und biotechnologische Prozesse. Sie wissen, wie sie durch gezieltes Eingreifen
Prozesse steuern und regeln können.
Fertigkeiten und Kompetenzen:
Die Studierenden sind in der Lage chemische oder biotechnologische Reaktionen mittels
Prozessmodellen zu beschreiben. Sie können die kinetischen Einflussgrößen auf den Prozess
erläutern und fachspezifisch bewerten. Dies befähigt sie zur Auswahl optimaler Betriebsweisen
und zur Entwicklung eigener Lösungen im fachlichen Rahmen gemäß der unter Wissen
und Verstehen angegebenen Inhalte. Dabei werden fachspezifische Gestaltungsregeln
eingehalten.
Nach erfolgreicher Teilnahme an der Vorlesung Stoffproduktion und Omics-Technologien
haben die Studierenden vertiefte Kenntnisse in den wichtigsten Produktionsbereichen
der Biotechnologie, den molekularbiologischen Möglichkeiten der Optimierung von
Produktionsprozessen sowie der Umweltbiotechnologie.
Wissen und Verstehen:
Die Studierenden haben spezifische fachbezogene Kenntnisse im Bereich der
biotechnologischen Produktion von Wertstoffen und der molekularbiologischen Optimierung
der Produktionsorganismen gewonnen: alkoholische Gärung, Wein, Bier, Vitamine, Antibiotika,
Pharmaproteine, Enzyme, organische Säuren, Polysaccharide, Steroide, Aromastoffe,

title: Biotechnology (In Depth Module)
text:
Biotechnology (In Depth Module) — content and learning objectives (part 4 of 4): Pharmaproteine, Enzyme, organische Säuren, Polysaccharide, Steroide, Aromastoffe,
Bodensanierung, Abwasserreinigung, Abluftreinigung, Omiktechnologien, Synthetische
Biologie, Tun-nelproteine, Systembiologie, Metabolic Engineering und Metagenom.
Fertigkeiten und Kompetenzen:
Die Studierenden sind in der Lage, Produktionsprozesse der Biotechnologie darzustellen und
die entsprechenden Prozesse zu erläutern sowie Optimierungsansätze zu den beschriebenen
Verfahren zu entwickeln.
Nach erfolgreicher Teilnahme an dem Praktikum haben die Studierenden grundlegende
Kenntnisse in den wichtigsten Verfahren der Fermentation von Mikroorganismen.
Wissen und Verstehen:
Die Studierenden haben spezifische fachbezogene Kenntnisse im Bereich der Isolation,
Charakterisierung und Fermentation von Mikroorganismen gewonnen. Insbesondere haben
sie die Schüttelkulturtechnik, batch, fed-batch und kontinuierliche Fermentationsverfahren,
wichtige fermentationstechnische Kenndaten, wichtige Analysemethoden sowie das Screening
auf Produktionsstämme kennengelernt.
Fertigkeiten und Kompetenzen:
Die Studierenden sind in der Lage, Produktionsprozesse der Biotechnologie und
Bioverfahrenstechnik darzustellen und die entsprechenden Prozesse zu erläutern und zu
modellieren sowie die beschriebenen Verfahren in die Praxis umzusetzen und sinnvolle
Ansätze für weitere Fermentationsverfahren zu entwerfen.

title: Cell and Molecular Biology of Plants
text:
Cell and Molecular Biology of Plants — content and learning objectives: a) Aspects of plant biochemistry using selected examples of signal perception and
transduction, epigenetics b) Structure and function of plant organelles, in-vivo-imaging,
reporter genes, methods for the molecular analysis of cellular processes c) Molecular
physiology of domesticated plants with an emphasis on the production of biomass d) Methods
of modern plant genetics and bioinformatics e) Molecular mechanisms of plant development
By combining theory with practical exercises the students will achieve a thorough
understanding of plant biochemistry, cell biology, developmental biology and physiology
(e.g. secondary metabolites, transport processes and mechanisms of signal transduction)
and obtain insights into modern bioanalytical techniques. Lectures and practical courses in
molecular genomics will provide basic knowledge and hands-on experience in bioinformatics.
Using host-pathogen interactions as an example, methods of disease diagnosis and research
in disease resistance will be practiced. In addition, general skills such as the evaluation and
interpretation of data, protocol writing, team work, time management, literature searches,
presentations and the application of bioinformatics programs will be taught. The lectures will be
accompanied by practical courses.

title: Project Module: Operation Research Practice Project
text:
Project Module: Operation Research Practice Project — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 1): In a team of 4-6 students of mathematics, computer science, data science, business
administration, economics, and (industrial) engineering, an optimization task originating from
or based on a company will have to be solved. “Solution” includes the complete process from
the discussion of the task with the ‘problem owners’ and the acquisition and preparation of real
data, through mathematical modeling, design of suitable algorithms and their implementation
on the computer, to evaluations and interpretations of the calculated solutions, their graphical
illustration and presentation to the ‘customers’.
Students can apply the theoretical knowledge acquired during their (OR) studies in a practical
situation. In particular, they can formalize and structure a practical optimization task and its
data, separate the essential from the non-essential; they can set up optimization models
that adequately describe the practical situation, search the literature for related problems
and classify them, apply and/or further develop algorithms, design and implement exact
and/or heuristic solution approaches themselves; they can design relevant scenarios for
computational studies, carry out the studies, and evaluate and present the results; students
can organize themselves in an interdisciplinary team; they can present the task, the solution
approach, the implementation, the results, the hurdles professionally, both for academic
experts as well as for practitioners

title: Project Module: Operation Research Practice Project
text:
Project Module: Operation Research Practice Project — prerequisites: Very good knowledge of linear and integer optimization, efficient algorithms, modeling
languages, modeling of practical tasks, etc, programming skills in C/C++ or Python important,
in-depth mathematical understanding and abstraction skills indispensable, willingness to
work intensively in an interdisciplinary team; broad disciplinary knowledge (production,
logistics, scheduling, routing, optimization methods, graph algorithms, heuristics, etc.) very
helpful (courses: Introduction to Operations Research, OR 1, and Practical Optimization
indispensable, helpful OR 2, useful OR 3)

title: Column Generation und Branch-and-Price
text:
Column Generation und Branch-and-Price — content and learning objectives: State-of-the-art of models and algorithms for solving very large-scale and complex optimization
problems, in particular column generation and branch-and-price; structured integer programs;
Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation; generalization to multiple subprobloms, Lagrange relaxation;
lower bounds, cutting planes in conjunction with column generation; branching rules; dual
variable stabilization; implementation details; practical applications.
Students expand their basic skills for modelling optimization problems to include advanced
modelling concepts (such as the use of configurational variables). They master the algorithmic
thinking to solve large linear and linear integer optimization models with decomposition
approaches based on Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation or Benders decomposition. These
algorithms should also be understood in practice when dealing with modeling languages,
for example. Students will be able to penetrate theoretical backgrounds and establish
relationships between them. The programming of column generation in an algorithmic
framework such as SCIP will be fundamentally learned. Students should be able to classify
and understand publications at the level of the current state of research and be able to transfer
their knowledge to practical problems.

title: Column Generation und Branch-and-Price
text:
Column Generation und Branch-and-Price — prerequisites: Essential: sound knowledge of linear/integer optimization from “Quantitative Methods” and
“Operations Research 1” (business administration, industrial engineering) and/or “efficient
algorithms” (computer science) and/or “integer linear optimization” (mathematics), i.e. in
particular mastery of duality of linear programs, branch-and-bound, modeling with integer
programs

title: Practical Optimization with Modeling Languages
text:
Practical Optimization with Modeling Languages — content and learning objectives: Es werden zunächst grundlegende, dann zunehmend komplexere und realistischere
Optimierungsprobleme mit Hilfe einer Modellierungssprache modelliert und gelöst (angefangen
von einfachen kombinatorischen Optimierungsproblemen wie Zuordnungsproblem,
Flussprobleme, Transportprobleme über Standortprobleme, Losgrößenplanung,
Tourenplanung, bis hin zu sehr aufwändigen Modellen mit exponentiell vielen Variablen und
Restriktionen, wie Set Partitioning Modelle für Crew Scheduling, Fahrzeugumlaufplanung,
etc.).
Knowledge
Die Studierenden lernen den praktischen Umgang mit einer Modellierungssprache.
Skills
Die Studierenden haben die Fähigkeit zum Modellieren von Optimierungsproblemen auch
realistischer Größe und Komplexität, "Modellierungstricks", und die Bedienung eines Lösers.
Competences
Sie können mit praktischen Datensätzen umgehen und Lösungen präsentieren.

title: Practical Optimization with Modeling Languages
text:
Practical Optimization with Modeling Languages — prerequisites: Lineare Optimierung und Modellieren mit Graphen sollte bekannt sein, etwa aus Einführung in
OR (QM), Operations Resarch 1 (AOR) oder Vergleichbarem.
Die Kenntnis einer Programmiersprache und generelle Fingerfertigkeit am Computer (Umgang
mit einem Texteditor, Eingabe von Befehlen auf der Konsole, etc.) ist sehr nützlich.

title: Operations Research 2
text:
Operations Research 2 — content and learning objectives: Mathematische Hintergründe, Vertiefungen und Ergänzungen zu den in "Operations Research
1" (in der Informatik heißt das Modul "Advanced Operations Research") gelehrten Inhalten,
insbesondere Komplexität von Problemen und Algorithmen, Polyeder-Theorie, ganzzahlige
Optimierung: total unimo-dulare Matrizen, TDI-Systeme, Schnittebenenverfahren; effiziente
Flussalgorithen und weiterführende Graphenalgorithmen
Die Studierenden erwerben eine vertiefte Kenntnis abstrakter, algorithmischer und struktureller
Zusammenhänge der linearen, ganzzahligen und diskreten Optimierung und das auch über
konkrete Anwendungen hinaus.

title: Operations Research 2
Capital Budgeting
text:
Capital Budgeting — content and learning objectives: This course deals with basic knowledge about capital budgeting. Major emphasis is given to
decisions based on net present value computations.
This course aims primarily at
1) imparting approaches to identify and structure basic financial decision problems,
2) fostering problem solving competencies by presenting and applying theoretical models
based on quantitative approaches in order to solve practical problems,
3) encouraging a stringent line of argument and critical questioning of different solution
approaches.
To be more specific, after successful participation, students will
1) know the basic assumptions of static and dynamic capital budgeting planning tools,
2) understand problems associated with decisions based on internal rates of return,
3) can apply and assess quantitative capital budgeting techniques for decisions under certainty
(e.g. on perfect or imperfect capital markets, with flat or non-flat yield curves, for one-shot or
repeated decisions) bearing in mind the underlying assumptions.

title: Portfolio Management
text:
Portfolio Management — content and learning objectives: In this course, students learn the basics of portfolio optimization in different decision-making
situations. Special attention is given to the problem of data acquisition.
The course focuses on developing the following skills in students: (1) The ability to solve
complex portfolio selection problems with the help of advanced methods of financial
management derived from the Markowitz portfolio theory. In doing so, stringent lines of
reasoning are fostered and the presented portfolio selection approaches are critically
questioned. (2) The capacity to assess the practical opportunities for data acquisition within the
framework of the Markowitz portfolio theory. (3) The knowledge which simplifying assumptions
facilitate the problem of data acquisition and how to evaluate these assumptions with regard
to their practical relevance. (4) The qualification to know and evaluate important alternative
portfolio selection approaches like maximizing the geometric mean of portfolio return or
considering shortfall-oriented risk measures (keyword: “value at risk”). Moreover, the course
emphasizes the importance of academic research for financial decision making and students
will learn how to develop new problem-solving approaches in a research-based way.

title: Portfolio Management
text: Portfolio Management — prerequisites: Basic knowledge in decision theory and statistics is expected or must be acquired individually.

title: Firm Valuation
text:
Firm Valuation — content and learning objectives: The theoretical foundations of modern firm evaluation on perfect and imperfect capital markets
are discussed. In addition, special questions are addressed, such as those concerning
the evaluation of small and medium-sized enterprises and possibilities for considering
sustainability aspects in firm evaluation.
Practical examples and case studies help to deepen the understanding. The evaluation
approaches are constantly critically assessed against their theoretical background.
Students acquire an advanced knowledge of the application of the state of the art in firm
valuation. In addition, they are able to assess critically the preconditions for the utilization
of these methods. Moreover, they get acquainted with ways of devising new research-
based problem solving strategies. In selected examples, students are made aware of
interdependencies between economic and ecological goals and their impact on firm valuation.

title: Firm Valuation
text:
Firm Valuation — prerequisites: Grundkenntnisse in Entscheidungslehre, Statistik, Investition und Finanzierung werden

title: Logistics Systems Planning I
text:
Logistics Systems Planning I — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Logistics planning aims at having the right item in the right quantity at the right time at the right
place at the right cost. The main drivers of logistics system costs are the design of the logistics
network, transportation, and warehouse operations. This course introduces the most important
planning tasks in these fields using mathematical modeling techniques and optimization
methods.
Transportation is responsible for a large part of worldwide CO2 emissions. The modeling
techniques and optimization methods taught in the course aim at minimizing transportation
costs, which is often simplified as a minimization of traveled distance in the respective
optimization models. Although the resulting solutions may not be optimal from an
emissions perspective, they provide large savings in emissions compared to manual
planning approaches. Thus, they represent an important step towards a more sustainable
transportation.
;
After the course, the students are able to:
- explain the main cost drivers in logistic systems and how optimization is used to reduce these
costs;
- describe the different transportation modes and their pros and cons
- recognize the complexity of logistics planning problems,
- model planning problems in network design, transportation and warehouse management,
- explain the advantages and disadvantages of different mathematical formulations and select
the most suitable formulation in a given decision scenario,

title: Logistics Systems Planning I
text:
Logistics Systems Planning I — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): the most suitable formulation in a given decision scenario,
- apply basic optimization methods to solve the described problems, and
- analyze and optimize a logistics system, especially with regard to transportation and
warehousing decisions

title: Logistics Systems Planning I
text:
Logistics Systems Planning I — prerequisites: Contentwise (recommended): Quantitative Methoden and/or Operations Research I and/or
Logistics Systems Planning I

title: Project Management
text:
Project Management — content and learning objectives: In this course, students learn about quantitative models and methods of project planning.
One focus is on the application and comparison of network planning techniques such as
the Critical Path Method (CPM), Metra Potential Method (MPM), Program Evaluation and
Review Technique (PERT), and Graphical Evaluation and Review Technique (GERT). In
addition, the course covers methods for minimizing costs in networks. It also shows how
project management-specific challenges in the areas of IT and logistics can be addressed.
After completing this module, students will be able to ...
... explain essential quantitative methods, models, and algorithms for project planning.
... apply software tools and manual procedures for calculating networks.
... explain essential methods of project management and their special features in the field of
logistics and IT projects.

title: Project Management

title: Managerial Accounting and Controlling

title: Operations Research 1
text:
Operations Research 1 — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): 1. Modelling with linear and integer programs: assignment problems, knapsack, facility location
problems, travelling salesperson problem, vehicle routing problem, scheduling problems, set
covering, set packing, set partitioning, bin packing, cutting stock, logical conditions;
2. Algorithms for integer programs: branch-and-bound, branch-and-cut, dynamic programming;
3. Fundamental heuristics and metaheuristics: construction and improvement heuristics,
greedy algorithms, local search, simulated annealing, tabu search;
4. Specific modelling situations such as soft constraints, non-linearities, heuristic modelling
Students learn how to model with linear (mixed) integer programs, how to define variables,
how to set up linear constraints and a linear objective function. In particular, students can
model logical conditions, selections, sequences, configurations with binary variables, represent
capacity conditions, represent time discretizations, model connectivity in graphs. As a result,
students can model basic problems such as flows, allocations, packing and cutting, location
planning, machine scheduling, lot size planning, routing problems, etc. as integer programs,
both concretely and abstractly. They can interpret constraints, specify and interpret solutions,
model simple unknown optimization problems independently and modify more complex,
known optimization problems. Students can classify the concept of the strength of a model

title: Operations Research 1
text:
Operations Research 1 — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): known optimization problems. Students can classify the concept of the strength of a model
and explain its importance in an algorithmic context. In particular, students are proficient in the
LP-based branch-and-bound algorithm, as well as basic extensions such as the cutting plane
algorithm or column generation, and simple dynamic programs. Students will be able to use
and read the necessary mathematical form with confidence.

title: Operations Research 1
text:
Operations Research 1 — prerequisites: Knowledge in the field of linear optimimization and basic graph algorithms, in particular
modeling with networks and linear programs is needed (and has to be acquired, if necessary,
in advance or during the semester)

title: International Financial Management
text:
International Financial Management — content and learning objectives: (1) Foreign exchange markets and exchange rates (basic knowledge as background for cross-
border financing, investment and currency management decisions)
(2) Basics of currency management (goals, instruments, (optimal) strategies for simple
decision-making situations)
(3) Cross-border capital budgeting decisions
(4) Financial decisions of multinational enterprises
Den Studierenden wird insbesondere das erforderliche Methodenwissen zur theoriegestützten,
quantitativen Lösung finanzwirtschaftlicher Entscheidungsprobleme im Zusammenhang
mit grenzüberschreitenden Unternehmensaktivitäten nahegebracht. Zudem werden den
Studierenden in diesem Zusammenhang die Identifikation und die Strukturierung komplexer
finanzwirtschaftlicher Entscheidungsprobleme vermittelt und ihre Fähigkeit zum kritischen
Hinterfragen der Voraussetzungen zum Einsatz der erörterten Methoden im Rahmen
stringenter Argumentationen geschult. Dabei werden die Studierenden in begrenztem Umfang
auch mit der Frage vertraut gemacht, wie forschungsbasiert neue Problemlösungsansätze
hergeleitet werden können, wodurch ein gewisses Fundament für eigene problemorientierte
Forschungsarbeiten geschaffen wird.

title: International Financial Management
text:

erwartet bzw. müssen angelesen werden.

title: Project Module: Analytics and Optimization Project
text:
Project Module: Analytics and Optimization Project — content and learning objectives: The Analytics and Optimization Project (AOP) is carried out in interdisciplinary groups
(economics, business administration, industrial engineering, mathematics, computer science)
of 3-6 students. Each group works on an application-oriented problem that can be solved
using methods from the areas of data analytics and operations research. In the past, the topics
were proposed by companies such as Ab Ovo Deutschland, AlixPartners, Barkawi, DHL, Flix,
Inform, Lufthansa, OptRail, Picnic and PTV. Each group is co-supervised by the company and
an RWTH research assistant, who provide support with literature research, implementation of
the solution procedure and preparation of the presentations.
After completing this course, students will be able to independently design and carry out simple
decision support and data analysis projects, i.e., (1) based on the description of a simple
planning or data analysis problem from business practice, develop a suitable solution method
as a combination of operations research and statistical data analysis methods they know, (2)
explain their method clearly to practitioners, (3) discuss its advantages and disadvantages in
the business context, (4) implement the necessary software, (5) carry out numerical studies to
evaluate the method, (6) visualize and interpret their results and transfer them to the practical
context in the form of recommendations.

title: Project Module: Analytics and Optimization Project
text:
Project Module: Analytics and Optimization Project — prerequisites: Basic knowledge of integer programming is essential, primarily the ability to model complex
optimization problems. The course is not suitable for students lacking these prerequisites.
Additionally, programming skills, practical experience with MIP solvers, prior knowledge of
construction heuristics, local search and metaheuristics as well as data analysis and statistics
are advantageous. The course requires the ability to work independently and autonomously.

title: Supply Chain Management
text:
Supply Chain Management — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): The course covers concepts, theories, and quantitative methods of interorganizational
collaboration in supply chains, with a focus on identifying and eliminating inefficiencies.
Topics include drivers and barriers of collaboration, coordination mechanisms, incentive
alignment, information sharing, and trust-building across organizational boundaries. The
course emphasizes output-oriented performance measures such as cost efficiency, revenue
generation, and customer satisfaction. Students analyze real-world case studies from various
industries to apply theoretical concepts, assess practical implementation challenges, and
develop a critical understanding of the success factors and potential pitfalls of collaborative
supply chain strategies.
After successful participation, students will have acquired the following skills and
competencies:
Students are able to solve complex interorganisational decision problems of modern value
chains with quantitative approaches. Emphasis is placed on enhancing firm performance
through cost reduction, revenue growth, and customer orientation. Real-world case studies
from various industries illustrate the practical relevance of the methods and will enable
students to critically evaluate collaborative strategies in different supply chain settings.
Wherever reasonable, students gain insights into ongoing research projects. This course
furthermore aspires to enable students in critical thinking about the applicability of the acquired

title: Supply Chain Management
text:
Supply Chain Management — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): furthermore aspires to enable students in critical thinking about the applicability of the acquired
methods. Students should be able to reason why a certain method is applicable (or not)
and they should be able to present its feasibility based on case studies. By the end of this
course, students will be able to formulate and critically analyze quantitative models for strategic
network design, inventory management, coordination, and revenue management.

title: Management of Enterprise Resource Planning and Interorganizational Information Systems
text:
Management of Enterprise Resource Planning and Interorganizational Information Systems — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Organizational information systems have been built and used for more than 50 years.
Throughout this period, such systems have steadily grown in complexity and size. While
initially systems were developed to support individual workers and then individual functional
departments, today?s systems often integrate all or most enterprise functions from
procurement to after-sales and from concept to marketing in one single database. Such
systems are called Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems. Moreover, such systems are
increasingly integrated between companies to form so-called inter-organizational information
systems (IOIS), for example for the purpose of improving supply chain management.
Due to their complexity and size, all but the largest user organizations find it beyond their
capability to develop the software required for these systems themselves. Therefore,
increasingly so-called off-the-shelf software is used to provide the core functionality around
which organizational information systems are built by configuring the software and by
embedding it in organizational procedures and practices and also by adding customized
software components. This process is called system implementation.
Using teaching cases, students will analyse real-life situations where implementation
processes of ERP-Systems and IOIS foundered or have been managed exceptionally well.
Students will have to present cases in class, preferably in teams, in which they also offer an

title: Information Management
text:
Information Management — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): The course deals with the design of an organizational information infrastructure by utilizing
both a decision theory as well as a practice theory based perspective. From a decision theory
perspective information management can be divided into strategic and operational tasks. The
strategic tasks include the long-term planning of the information infrastructure through the
determination of general design parameters, e.g. companywide standards, and the strategic
selection of projects aimed at the development of certain information systems. The operational
tasks generally include the implementation and operation of information systems. During the
course, different techniques for successful strategic and operational information management
from the literature are introduced and critically discussed. From a practice theory perspective
the main objective of information management is to exert a purposeful influence on practices of
IT use. The first and foremost question in this context is whether the information infrastructure
of an organization can be purposefully manipulated at all. Given the highly routinized character
of IT use in organizations, practices of use become the central design parameter of information
management. The possibilities and limits of the purposeful change of practices of use will be
discussed with the help of selected case studies on the topic. Finally, the course deals with the

title: Information Management
text:
Information Management — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): discussed with the help of selected case studies on the topic. Finally, the course deals with the
topic of information infrastructures as a means of strategic positioning and differentiation in a
world characterized by universal IT use and ubiquitous information systems.
Students get to know the main instruments of strategic and operational information
management and learn how to critically evaluate their applicability.
Furthermore, they can recognize theoretical concepts of information management in concrete
decision and design situations and are able to develop proposals as to their use.

title: Development of IT Standards
text:
Development of IT Standards — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Organizations are the main buyers of information technology (IT) products. Such products
are used to build information systems which increasingly cross organizational boundaries.
Information systems consist not only of IT products, but also of organizational processes,
knowledge and rules. Together, they form the "nervous system" of organizations and networks
of organizations. From a user’s point of view, this means that IT products need to be integrated
as components into larger systems; from a vendor’s point of view, products need to be
positioned so as to make their incorporation into larger systems easy while also protecting
competitive interests of the firm. The key to both these tasks is the specification and possibly
standardization of interfaces through which IT products are linked with other products and
systems, thus becoming part of systems themselves. Therefore, consideration of possible
participation in processes aimed at specifying and standardizing these interfaces becomes
an increasingly important task for vendors and user organizations alike (often, large vendors
are also users themselves). Thus, the field of IT standardization is well on its way towards
becoming a general management issue.
The course consists of a theoretical and an empirical part. The theoretical part addresses
basic conceptual issues and then proceeds to analyze market-based and committee-based
standardization processes as well as the effectiveness of standardization processes. It also

title: Development of IT Standards
text:
Development of IT Standards — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): standardization processes as well as the effectiveness of standardization processes. It also
introduces a more fine-grained typology of standardization processes. The theoretical part
concludes with presenting an integrated model of standardization processes which will then be
used to analyze several cases that are all drawn from the area of wireless data communication
systems.
The course will rely on published case studies of real-life IT standardization processes.
Students will have to present and analyze individual cases, preferably in teams. Cases will
revolve around one specific technology (mobile telecommunications) so as to facilitate a basic
understanding of the technical issues involved in the standardization processes selected
for this course. The course consists of regular classes and tutorials. Tutorials will be used
to refresh basic concepts in organizational and economic theory as well as provide a basic
understanding of technical concepts used in this course.
In this course, students will learn to
(1) appreciate the relevance of IT standardization processes for organizations;
(2) understand and analyze standardization processes;
(3) evaluate such standardization processes from the perspective of firms (both as users and
vendors of IT).
(4) develop a critical attitude towards literature.

title: IT and Organisation
text:
IT and Organisation — content and learning objectives: In this course organizational effects of information technology (IT) use are examined at
different levels of analysis, particularly the macro, sector, and the organizational network level
as well as the level of the single organization and the organization of work processes.
Different effects will be examined depending on the level of analysis, e.g. productivity at the
macro level or the degree of job specialization at the level of work organization.
The course consists of lecture and exercise. In the lecture, students will give lectures on
selected topics. In the exercise, selected aspects from the fields of organizational theory
and business informatics are dealt with in order to compensate for knowledge gaps. This is
necessary because the course has no prerequisites regarding economics content.
Teilnehmer des Kurses werden lernen,
(1) Grundformen der Organisation wirtschaftlicher Tätigkeiten (divisionale und funktionale
Organisation, Lieferketten, Cluster) zu unterscheiden;
(2) grundlegende Formen des IT-Einsatzes in wirtschaftlichen Organisationen zu erkennen
und zu beschreiben (ERP-Systeme, elektronischen Geschäftsdatenaustausch, elektronische
Märkte);
(3) den heutigen Stand der wissenschaftlichen Forschung zu der Frage der Auswirkungen von
IT auf die Organisation wirtschaftlicher Tätigkeiten kritisch zu reflektieren.

title: Mathematical System Theory 1
text:
Mathematical System Theory 1 — content and learning objectives: ● Introduction to Control
● Classical methods to solve ordinary differential equations (ODE)
● Laplace transform
● Modelling
● System Dynamics of first and second order systems
● System Dynamics of Closed-loop Systems
● Frequency Response and Bode plots
● Stability, Hurwitz and Routh-Hurwitz criteria
● Nyquist Criterion, Gain Margin, Phase Margin
● Design of Control Loops in time and frequency domain, lag-lead compensation (2 lectures)
● Cascaded Control and Feedforward Compensation
● Root Locus Analysis and Design
Students shall gain a basic understanding for signals and systems allowing them to solve real-
world technical problems using the mathematical tools and concepts provided in SYST 1
● In the lecture “Systemtheorie 1 - Control Systems Engineering”, analogue signals and
systems are focused.
● Students shall be introduced to Laplace transform as a major tool for analysis and design of
linear single-input single-output systems.
● Students shall obtain a basic understanding of modelling for physical systems using ODEs
and block diagrams.
● Students shall get a more detailed introduction to the properties of first and second order
systems.
● Students shall learn the concept of feedback and its impact on systems. Students shall be
able to analyze and design control loops.
● Students shall be able to analyze the stability of given system configurations using the
methods covered in class.

title: Mathematical System Theory 2
text:
Mathematical System Theory 2 — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Ein- und Ausgangsbeschreibung zeitdiskreter Systeme, Operatorenrechnung für zeitdiskrete
Systeme: Elementare Körpertheorie, Operatorenkörper, V-Transformation, Anwendung der
Operatorenrechnung, Zusammenhang z-Transformation und Operatorenrechnung.
Analyse von Abtastsystemen: Quasikontinuierliche Abtastregelungen, Parameteroptimierte
Regelalgorithmen, Stabilität zeitdiskreter Systeme.
Systembeschreibung und Analyse im Zustandsraum, Zustand und Zustandsvariable: Zustand,
Übergangsfunktion, Ausgangsfunktion. Systemdynamik und lokale Übergangsfunktion
zeitdiskreter und zeitkontinuierlicher Systeme.
Aufstellen der Zustandsgleichungen aus der Übertragungsfunktion: Regelungsnormalform,
Beobachternormalform, Jordansche Normalform; äquivalentes zeitdiskretes Modell
im Zustandsraum. Lösung der Zustandsgleichungen für lineare zeitdiskrete Systeme.
Erreichbarkeit, Steuerbarkeit und Beobachtbarkeit linearer Systeme, Duale Systeme.
Äquivalente Systeme: Ähnliche Systeme; Zerlegung in Unterräume,
Basistransformationsmatrix, minimale äquivalente Systeme.
Regelung im Zustandsraum: Struktur einer Zustandsregelung, Regelungssynthese im
Zustandsraum, Schätzung des Zustandsvektors.
Kalman-Filter: Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung, Modell des gestörten Systems ohne
Rückführung, Ableitung des Kalman-Filters, Zustandsschätzung des gestörten Systems mit
Rückführung, Eigenschaften des Kalman-Filters.
Adaptive Systeme: adaptive Systemmodelle, Adaptionsalgorithmen, adaptiver Beobachter.

title: Mathematical System Theory 2
text:
Mathematical System Theory 2 — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): Rückführung, Eigenschaften des Kalman-Filters.
Adaptive Systeme: adaptive Systemmodelle, Adaptionsalgorithmen, adaptiver Beobachter.
● Die Studierenden sind in der Lage, Systeme mit Hilfe der Zustandsdarstellung zu
beschreiben, das Verhalten und die Stabilität zu analysieren und Regelungen im
Zustandsraum zu entwerfen, so dass das Systemverhalten vorgegebene Anforderungen erfüllt.
Sie verstehen die Vor- und Nachteile der verschiedenen Normalformen und können zeigen, ob
Modelle ähnliche Systeme beschreiben können. Sie wissen, wie der Systemzustand für eine
Regelung geschätzt werden kann, wenn er nicht direkt messbar ist.
● Darüber hinaus wird in Systemtheorie 2 die stochastische Beschreibung von Signalen
eingeführt, die im Gegensatz zu der z.B. in Systemtheorie 1 verwendeten deterministischen
Beschreibung kein exaktes Wissen über den eigentlichen Signalverlauf, sondern nur über
seine stochastischen Eigenschaften verlangt. Nach erfolgreicher Teilnahme haben die
Studierenden ein Verständnis für stochastische Signale und ihre Beschreibung durch Größen
wie z.B. Verteilung und Korrelationsfunktion erwerben. Darauf basierend können sie die
Strukturen und Eigenschaften von Kalman Filtern und adaptiven Regelungen verstehen und
diese für lineare Systeme entwerfen

title: Power Electronics - Fundamentals, Topologies and Analysis
text:
Power Electronics - Fundamentals, Topologies and Analysis — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): Die Veranstaltung befasst sich mit der Steuerung und der effizienten Umformung elektrischer
Energie mit Hilfe leistungselektronischer Schalter. Anwendungsgebiete sind z. B. elektrische
Antriebs- und Stromversorgungssysteme im Automobilbereich, verteilte Stromerzeugung
mittels Windkraftanlagen, Sonnenenergie oder Brennstoffzellen, Batteriesysteme, industrielle
Antriebe, induktive Erwärmung sowie Leistungsflussregelung im Energieerzeugermaßstab
und Gleichstromübertragungssysteme. Die Vorlesung stellt zunächst Funktionsweisen und
Topologien netzgeführter sowie selbstgeführter Stromrichter vor. Netzgeführte Stromrichter,
welche mit der Frequenz des angeschlossenen Drehstrom- oder Wechselstromnetzes
schalten, werden anhand wichtiger Anwendungen wie Umkehrstromrichter und Direktumrichter
vorgestellt. Ein eigenes Kapitel ist den Netzrückwirkungen gewidmet. Selbstgeführte
Stromrichter, wie Gleichstromsteller sowie strom- und spannungseinprägende Wechselrichter
werden mit besonderem Fokus auf verschiedenen Steuer- und Regelverfahren, wie z. B.
Stromregelung und Pulsdauermodulationsverfahren, betrachtet. Ein Skript ist erhältlich.
Nach der erfolgreichen Teilnahme an den Modulveranstaltungen sind die Studierenden in der
Lage,
● die Grundlagen der Umformung elektrischer Energie durch Halbleiterschalter zu verstehen,
● grundlegende Umrichtertopologien zu identifizieren und deren Funktionsweise zu verstehen,

title: Electrodynamics - Electromagnetic Waves
text:
Electrodynamics - Electromagnetic Waves — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): The complete system of Maxwell's equations – Poynting's theorem – quickly changing fields
– Maxwell's equations for arbitrary and for harmonic time dependence – polarization of fields
– telegraph equation – wave equation – Helmholtz equation – wave propagation in unbound,
homogeneous, isotropic media – plane waves – parameters of waves – phase, group and
energy velocity – power flux and energy in a quickly changing field – introduction of the
Poynting vector S – reflection and transmission of a plane, harmonic wave at a boundary –
skin effect – electrodynamic potentials (retarded potentials) – decomposition in TE and TM
waves – wave propagation in wave guides – Hertzian dipole – solution of boundary value
problems for fields with harmonic time dependence – solution of the Helmholtz equation
via separation of variables – adjusting of solutions to boundary conditions – solution of two-
dimensional problems – TEM wave guides – telegrapher's equations
After successful participation the students are able to:
● understand fundamental electrodynamic problems and apply Maxwell's equations to them,
● choose the required methods from vector calculus and apply them,
● analyze the propagation of plane waves in vacuum and homogeneous matter,
● calculate the influence of reflection and transmission at a planar boundary on wave
propagation,
● relate the problem of a guided wave tot he corresponding boundary value problem,

Mastering the inner workings of basic models and algorithms formulate their implementation
in unconventional physical, brain-like substrates. Fostering a cross-disciplinary thinking and
communicationacross related science areas: electrical engineering, neuroscience, physics,
computer science etc.

title: Brain-inspired Computing and Engineering
text:
Brain-inspired Computing and Engineering — prerequisites: Basic proficiency in coding (Python, Matlab, etc.)is required. For course projects, it will be
beneficial tohave either more advanced coding or electrical circuits (e.g., Spice simulations)
proficiency.

title: DSP Design Methodologies and Tools
text:
DSP Design Methodologies and Tools — content and learning objectives: • Introduction: Definition of embedded systems; design challenges; design
methodologies
• System design: System design methodologies; requirements and specifications
• Instruction sets: Basic classification of computer architecture; assembly language;
examples of software assembly instruction-set
• Microprocessors: Various I/O mechanism; supervisor mode, exceptions, traps; co-
processor
• Designing with microprocessors: Architectures and components (software, hardware);
debugging; manufacturing testing
• Program design & analysis: Design patterns; representation of programs; assembling,
linking
• VLSI implementation: Importance of VLSI; Moore's Law; VLSI design process
• RTL components: Shifters; adders; multipliers
• Architecture and chip design: Basics of register-transfer design; data path, controller;
ASM chart; VHDL, Verilog overview
• EDA systems and algorithms: EDA systems; placement and routing; layout analysis
The students will acquire a basic understanding of the design of embedded signal processing
systems.
At the end of the module students are able
• to construct system-level models using abstract specification languages such as
StateCharts.
• to develop optimized software for Digital Signal Processors in C and assembly
language and to implement simple combinational and sequential digital hardware
circuits using the
• VHDL hardware description language.

title: DSP Design Methodologies and Tools
text: DSP Design Methodologies and Tools — prerequisites: Basic C or assembly programming capabilities

title: Automation of Complex Power Systems
text:
Automation of Complex Power Systems — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 2): • Distribution grid automation: fundamentals, prerequisites, and historical perspective
• Distribution grid automation and control
• Power system protection and protection automation
• Distributed energy resources and integration of renewables
• Microgrids
• Standards for distribution grid automation
• Data models, and standards for power systems
• Communication systems for power systems
• Demand side management and flexibility concepts
• Advanced converter-based control methods
• Applications of power system contro
At the end of the module, students are able:
• to understand and apply the basic principles of distribution grid automation, including
its underlying motivation, historical development, and main functional layers,
• to explain automation, monitoring, control, and protection functions in modern
distribution grids,
• to explain the role of communication systems, data models, common standards, and
the Common Information Model (CIM) in power system automation,
• to apply basic feedback control and state-space modeling concepts to selected power
system automation problems,
• to analyze voltage and frequency control mechanisms in automated power systems,
• to assess the impact of distributed energy resources, renewable generation, demand-
side management, and grid codes on distribution grid operation,
• to describe microgrid operation and control concepts for grid-connected and islanded
operation,

title: Automation of Complex Power Systems
text:
Automation of Complex Power Systems — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 2): • to describe microgrid operation and control concepts for grid-connected and islanded
operation,
• to explain advanced converter-based control principles, including instantaneous power
and synchronverter concepts.

title: Advanced Control Systems
text:
Advanced Control Systems — content and learning objectives: • Basics of muliple-input-multiple-output (MIMO) systems and representations
• Analysis of MIMO-systems, modelling of uncertainties
• General control configuration, robustness and performance
• H2- (LQR/LQG) control
• Introduction to robust H∞-control
• Implementation aspects of robust controllers
• μ-synthesis
Students develop an advanced understanding of modern methods of linear feedback control.
This includes the application of modern multiple-input-multiple output (MIMO) system analysis
and tools for feedback controller design in such complex systems with uncertainties. Students
learn to understand and apply state-space and frequency domain methods for MIMO systems.

title: Advanced Control Systems
text:
Advanced Control Systems — prerequisites: Relevant and finished Bachelor level studies, control engineering 1 and 2 (frequency response
and state-space methods) or similar introductory courses to control engineering.

title: Digitalization of Energy Distribution Grids
text:
Digitalization of Energy Distribution Grids — content and learning objectives (part 1 of 3): The new assets installed in energy distribution grids for electricity, gas and heat as part of the
energy transition lead
to increased complexity in its planning and operation.
Fundamentals of safe and efficient operation of future energy systems are digitization, the
constant exchange of data and the availability of process data between different stakeholders
of the energy supply systems. However, managing the digitization in critical infrastructures
requires a differentiated view of several categories. Measurement and control technology is
connected to grid control systems by information and communication technology and bundled
there. Furthermore, security infrastructure and other use cases are also of great importance.
In the course of the lecture, an overview of digitalization in electrical and other energy
distribution networks is given.
In the introduction, the basics of power systems and digitalization topics such as measurement
and communication
technology are given. This content is necessary to understand the application related content
of the later lecture blocks.
After the basics, individual topics of digitalization of energy systems are covered in detail.
Measurement and control
systems are essential for the control of various flexible systems. Here, methods for automated
processing of large amounts of data such as edge computing are necessary. Various
communication technologies form the backbone of

title: Digitalization of Energy Distribution Grids
text:
Digitalization of Energy Distribution Grids — content and learning objectives (part 2 of 3): processing of large amounts of data such as edge computing are necessary. Various
communication technologies form the backbone of
the digitalized grids, while specialized software such as grid control systems provide the
necessary human-machine
interface. Driven by these developments and current incidents, IT security is also increasingly
coming into focus in the digitalization process.
Finally, the topics are linked to application areas. In particular, the topics of grid planning, data
analysis and asset
management will be considered
Upon completion of the event series, students will be able to:
• explain the challenges of the energy transition in energy distribution grids
• explain the background of the digitalization in energy distribution grids
• understand the challenges of digitalized plants in energy systems
• evaluate and differentiate the regulatory background and hurdles of digitalization in
Germany in comparison to other countries
• describe the possible applications of flexibilities and controllable systems
• understand the basics of measurement and control technology as well as information
and communication technology in the context of modern distribution networks
• describe the functionality of measurement systems, e.g. smart meters as well as other
grid sensors
• explain possibilities for processing large amounts of data in measurement systems
(e.g. edge computing)
• explain the functionality of control systems in distribution grids, e.g. on-load-tap

title: Digitalization of Energy Distribution Grids
text:
Digitalization of Energy Distribution Grids — content and learning objectives (part 3 of 3): (e.g. edge computing)
• explain the functionality of control systems in distribution grids, e.g. on-load-tap
changer (OLTC) transformers and decentral voltage regulation (Q(U) controllers)
• describe various communication systems and protocols, e.g. SCADA and smart meter
gateway (SMGW) and weigh their advantages and disadvantages against each other
• describe the structure and purpose of grid control systems
• describe the basics and requirements of IT security in critical infrastructures
• understand the possibility of using neural networks in grid planning and operation
 
• pre-process, analyze and visualize large data sets with an energy context
• enumerate the possibilities for using machine learning methods in asset management
• create simple control loops
• apply statistical methods in the subject area of power engineering (statistical
quantities, measurement errors and their distributions, and error propagation)

title: Digitalization of Energy Distribution Grids

title: Numerical Analysis III
text:
Numerical Analysis III — content and learning objectives: Numerische Methoden für gewöhnliche Differentialgleichungen und Algebro-
Differentialgleichungen
Die Studierenden sollen Verständnis für grundlegende Prinzipien bei der Diskretisierung
von gewöhnlichen und Algebro-Differentialgleichungen entwickeln, grundlegende Techniken
wie Ein- und Mehrschrittverfahren, Schrittweitensteuerung, Extrapolation und semiimplizite
sowie implizite Ansätze sicher beherrschen, Grundbegriffe und Konzepte wie die Steifigkeit
eines Problems und die Stabilität eines Algorithmus durchdringen, die Fähigkeit vertiefen,
grundlegende numerische Methoden in ihrer Funktionsweise zu verstehen, die durch sie
erreichbaren Ergebnisse einzuschätzen und darauf aufbauend in flexibler Anpassung an
neue Aufgabenstellungen die Methode weiter zu entwickeln und aufbauend auf diesen
methodischen Werkzeugen weitere grundlegende Konzepte für das approximative Lösen
wissenschaftlicher und technischer Probleme aneignen.

title: Numerical Analysis III

title: Numerical Analysis IV

entwickeln, Verständnis für grundlegende Prinzipien bei der Diskretisierung von partiellen
Differentialgleichungen und bei der Optimierung entwickeln, grundlegende numerische
Methoden in ihrer Funktionsweise vertieft verstehen, Grundtechniken wie Finite-Differenzen
Verfahren, iterative Lösungsverfahren und Optimierungsmethoden sicher beherrschen und die
Fähigkeit zum aktiven Umgang mit den Gegenständen der Lehrveranstaltung erwerben und
Verständnis für die angemessenen Stabilitätsbegriffe entwickeln.

title: Optimization A
text:
Optimization A — content and learning objectives: Optimality Criteria for Constraint and Unconstraint Problems, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker Theory,
Parametric and Semi-infinite Optimization, Konvexity, Duality, Separation Theorems, Linear
Systems of inequalities, Constraint Qualifications, Linear Optimization, Simplex Method,
Ellipsoid Algorithm of Khachyan, Karmarkar Algorithm. Gradient and Newton Method, SQP
Method, Conjugate Directions/Gradients, Nonsmooth Optimization, Bundle Methods, Inner
Point Methods, Homotopy Methods, Introduction to Morse Theorie

Knowledge of the most important algorithmic methods and structural theorems in discrete

complexity

Differentialgleichungen (z.B. Variationsprobleme, Lagrange- Multiplikatortheoreme,

Die Studierenden sollen die Grundlagen der harmonischen Analysis am Beispiel der

die algebraische Analyse von Differentialgleichungen entwickeln, eine praxisnahe Anwendung
der Linearen Algebra kennenlernen, die Theorie der Moduln über Hauptidealringen an einem
konkreten Fall vertiefen.

Ringe, Moduln, Körper erwerben, das Zusammenspiel algebraischer Begriffsbildungen
kennenlernen, an mindestens einem Beispiel eine Strukturtheorie vertiefen, den Bezug der

title: Computational Mixed Integer Programming
text:
Computational Mixed Integer Programming — content and learning objectives: (1)Modellierung mit binären und ganzzahligen Variablen,
(2) Modellierungssprachen wie ZIMPL und GAMS,
(3) Branch-and-Bound, Branch-and-Cut, Branch-and-Price,
(4) MIP Löser: Preprocessing, Branchingregeln, Knotenauswahl, Primalheuristiken,
(5) Dekompositionstechniken wie Lagrange Relaxation, Spaltengenerierung
(6) Schnittebenentechniken. Die Veranstaltung besteht je zur Hälfte aus Vorlesung und
Programmierübung am Computer.
In der Veranstaltung wird an den Stand der Technik bei algorithmischen und
programmiertechnischen Fragestellungen der rechnerischen Lösung gemischt-ganzzahliger
Programme herangeführt. Die TeilnehmerInnen sollen in die Lage versetzt werden, eine
geeignete Kombination von Modell und Algorithmus zu finden oder zu entwickeln, um
für komplexe kombinatorische Optimierungsprobleme Optimallösungen oder Lösungen
beweisbarer Güte berechnen zu können. Ein unverzichtbarer Schwerpunkt ist dabei die
Kenntnis des internen Aufbaus moderner Lösungssoftware.

title: Computational Mixed Integer Programming
text:

lineare/ganzzahlige Optimierung, wichtig ist das sichere Beherrschen einer höheren

title: Integer Linear Optimization
text:
Integer Linear Optimization — content and learning objectives: Polyedertheorie, Schnittebenenverfahren, Äquivalenz von Optimierung und Separierung,
Branch und Bound Verfahren, Gomory Schnitte, Mixed Integer Rounding, Lagrangian
Relaxierung, Bender’s Zerlegung, Spaltengenerierung und Branch und Price, spezielle
(gemischt-) ganzzahlige Probleme, Optimierungssoftware.
Die Studierenden sollen Verständnis für die ganzzahlige lineare Optimierung vertiefen und die
fortgeschrittenen Methoden zum Lösen von (gemischt-) ganzzahligen Programmen kennen
und anwenden können.

lokale Körper, p-adische Zahlen
Die Studierenden sollen neue algebraische Objekte kennenlernen und mit ihnen rechnen,
diverse Computeralgebrasysteme benutzen, gelernte algebraische Konzepte anwenden,
vertiefte Kenntnisse im strukturellen Zugang zur Mathematik erwerben, Grundlagen zum
eigenständigen wissenschaftlichen Arbeiten erlernen, Grundwissen erlangen, das sie befähigt,
weiterführende wissenschaftliche Originalarbeiten zu lesen, Basiswissen und Fertigkeiten für
die Abschlussarbeit und das weitere Studium erwerben.

Die Studierenden sollen die Grundzüge der Gruppentheorie kennenlernen, vertiefte

zur Prämienkalkulation, Rückversicherungsverträge, Grundlagen der Risikotheorie und
Ruinwahrscheinlichkeiten
Die Studierenden sollen Kenntnis und Verständnis der grundlegenden Ergebnisse und
Methoden der Versicherungsmathematik erwerben, Wesen und Zielsetzung stochastischer
Modelle verstehen, Modelle anwenden und Aussagen in Modellen bewerten und interpretieren
können, Lösungsstrategien für gestellte Aufgaben und praktische Anforderungen entwickeln
und umsetzen können, mit dieser Veranstaltung ein sicheres Fundament für Anwendungen der
Versicherungsmathematik erwerben.

Entscheidungstheorie, grundlegende Konzepte der mathematischen Statistik (Schätz- und
Testtheorie, Suffizienz, Vollständigkeit)
Die Studierenden sollen Kenntnis und Verständnis der grundlegenden Begriffe und Prinzipien
der mathematischen Statistik erwerben, lernen, die zentralen Konzepte und Methoden
der Stochastik zielgerichtet und sicher anzuwenden, Aussagen der Statistik bewerten
und interpretieren können, Wesen und Zielsetzung stochastischer Modelle verstehen,
stochastische Modelle nachvollziehen und selbst entwickeln sowie das Arbeiten in einem

Anwendungen der Statistik erwerben.

Die Studierenden sollen Kenntnis und Verständnis der grundlegenden Ergebnisse und
Methoden der Erneuerungstheorie erwerben, Wesen und Zielsetzung stochastischer Modelle
verstehen, Modelle anwenden und Aussagen in Modellen bewerten und interpretieren können,
Lösungsstrategien für gestellte Aufgaben und praktische Anforderungen entwickeln und
umsetzen können, mit dieser Veranstaltung ein sicheres Fundament für Anwendungen der
Erneuerungstheorie erwerben.

title: Partial Differerential Equations

2. Galerkin Technik, Lax-Milgram
3. Finite-Elemente-Verfahren für elliptische Probleme
4. Moderne iterative Verfahren: PCG, Mehrgittermethode

6. Finite-Volumen-Methode
